our children love each other. I see how they play together. They have
such a sweet little game. Anatole is very fond of his old master. And
the others are not so devoted. You will forgive me, my dear friend,
but I wish Anatole and I were only one child, and he and I would play
together. I know how precious your father is. I know he helped you and
you helped him. He was a noble man, an orderly man, a good man. He
would not have you become a coward, a miser, a slave, a fool. He
was a man of virtue. He loved you. He loved me. But he died.”

“Your father,” continued Anna Pávlovna with shuddering
conviction, “was the most perfect man on earth. Forgive me, my dear
friend, but this is impossible. It is not possible to say that a man
is perfect. He who is perfect is a miracle. He must have been a
miracle in order to be a perfect man. And if he were not perfect, a
perfect man would have been a miracle, and the boundary between the
miracle and the perfect man would be lost. ‘What is a perfect man?’
that is the first and most difficult question to answer. A perfect
man is a paradox. He is both a miracle and an impossibility, two
contradictories in one.”

“Ah,” said the prince, “that is true enough. If there was a perfect
man, there would not be the perfect man.”

“Why not?”

“I don’t know,” said the prince, “but I think that if there were a
perfect man we should have a perfect world. If I were a perfect man,
then there would be no base humanity in the world. If I were a
perfect man I would take care of all. I would not despise a human being
who was a woman. I would not despise a human being who was a man. I
would never do a wicked thing. I would never allow anybody to do a
wicked thing. I would never be a hypocrite. I would never be a
disgrace. I would never flatter myself.”

Anna Pávlovna, with a suppressed smile, shook her head.

“But if there were a perfect man, we would live in a perfect world,”
replied the prince.

“I don’t know,” said the lady, “but I think that if there were a
perfect man, we would have a perfect world. It is not easy to say
whether it is possible or impossible to be a perfect man. I know that
you are a perfect man. And will you be a perfect man? If you were a
perfect man, would you be a perfect father? Would you abandon the
world and not desire anything? Would you not have any desire? Would
you not be afraid of death? Would you not wish to live long? Would
you not be afraid of the devil? I don’t know. I don’t know.”

The prince was silent. He did not know what to say. But Anna Pávlovna
thought that she had not been quite clear and resumed:

“Do you know how I sometimes think about you, my dear friend? If you
were a perfect man, you would not have this illness, this grippe,
this cough.”

The prince took up his hat, rose, turned hastily out of the room, and
was going to leave.

“I should have been at the English ambassador’s this morning,” said he
as he went out.

“You will be there,” said Anna Pávlovna, “and if you don’t see me,
I shall think you have forgotten me.”

With a confused, unsteady step, the prince walked out to the
streets.

The next day he went to the English ambassador’s and was received by
his faithful servant, the well-known and esteemed Wintzingerode.

He went to the English ambassador’s without any one following him, but
the gate was opened by one of the English servants. He was warmly
received, and was greeted by the good old man, who said:

“Excuse me, sir. I am a little late, I am sorry,” and he bowed to the
prince.

The good old man was the very same man whom Prince Vasíli had met once
in St. Petersburg. He was tall and well-built and had a round face and
large, intelligent eyes. He was a big, good man, with a great
sense of honor and long experience but without any ambition.

He was a good friend of Prince Vasíli and had always known him
well. He had been member of all the customs committees of the
Emperor. He was an indisputable man of the first rank, and the
prince had given him a very great confidence. This old friend of the
prince was in fact the most faithful and yet the most indifferent of
all his acquaintances, and he always behaved towards the prince with
a kindly, but aloof, cold, and sometimes even downright distrustful
manners.

He was a man whose character was highly estimable, and it was only
just that he should be, but not easily approachable. He was of a high
type and of a good and noble nature. His heart was warm and his
soul was pure. He was a man of great intelligence, a man with a great
sense of honor, and a man who was always and everywhere conscious of
the truth. He was a man of great knowledge and of great moral
prudence, and he had every reason to believe that he had good
intention. But he seemed to have a very great and avowedly high
ideal, and this ideal made him indifferent and aloof.

“Can I see you?” asked the prince.

“Yes, sir, I am here.”

free man. You are a man of character and of your own mind. You are a
great man, but you are not such a great man!”

The prince was silent, and for a moment the woman who had been
contemplating life with her eyes turned from him to the floor. But she
rose and continued:

“I am going to say that I know you well and have known you from
childhood. I know your character and I have heard you speak of yourself
to me in private. You are a great man, and I have been amazed at
your courage and your invincible faith. But you cannot have everything
you desire. You will have to wait, and you will not have to wait
together with me, and I will not be able to do much to help you. You
will have to wait in the world and in your own heart. You will have to
wait for a child to be born. But I can do nothing to hasten your
expectation. In this way life is not cruel to you, but has to wait for
its own course. You are right, however, in thinking that it is a
great pity that Anatole is not married. The world is cruel to me
because I don’t know what to do with her, and I don’t know how to
give her love. I can’t marry her. I want to marry her, but for her
alone.”

The prince answered nothing; but he was silent, and the atmosphere
between them was filled with a heavy, melancholy atmosphere.

“Now,” said Anna Pávlovna, “don’t ask me what I am going to say. I
want you to hear it. What I am going to say is true, but you won’t
believe it. I am going to say that I am a bad woman. I am going to say
that I have no more faith left in the world. I have given up all
hope. You will see me mad. I am going to say that I have no more faith
left in the world. I have given up all hope. I am a bad woman.”

The prince was silent again.

“I am going to say that I am a bad woman. I am going to say that I
have no more faith left in the world.”

She made a gesture of despair, and then she added:

“I am going to say that nothing is possible without faith. Faith is
the only foundation of society. All those who live without faith are
destroying society. I will not let myself be destroyed, I will not
allow myself to be driven into despair and madness. I cannot give up
my faith. I will not let myself be driven to despair. The Empress,
and all who have any sense, must believe in the great, and the
worship of the great must be made glorious. The Empress, the Empress
alone, must be the great. Everyone else must believe in her. She must
be the first great and the greatest. Only she can give hope to the
people. Only she can save the world.”

There was a silence, and Anna Pávlovna at last broke it by saying:

“I think that I will marry Anatole,” and she added, and then
remained speechless, and the prince was silent.

“What do you think?” she asked.

“I have no opinion,” said the prince.

“You think nothing?” she asked.

“I have no opinion,” he answered.

But he did not look at her at all.

“Why?” she asked.

“I have no opinion,” he said again.

“This is just what you say,” said Anna Pávlovna; “but you are not
so good a man as you think. I know you well, and you are not a man who
can say nothing. How can I ever trust you?”

She turned her head and looked at him, and then she said:

“If you don’t tell me that this means war, if you still try to
defend the infamies and horrors perpetrated by that Antichrist—I
really believe he is Antichrist—I will have nothing more to do with
you and you are no longer my friend, no longer my faithful slave, as
you call yourself! But how do you do? I see I have frightened you—sit
down and tell me all the news.”

The prince turned to Anna Pávlovna with a smile.

“In the meantime I must go to the English ambassador’s to be there
tonight,” he said.

“I am going too,” said Anna Pávlovna. “I shall be very glad to
see you.”

She went to the door, and as she was opening it the prince stopped her
and asked:

“What is it?”

“What does it matter to me? I shall be very glad to see you.”

“Very glad?” asked the prince.

“What do you mean?” she asked.

Perhaps it is nothing, but unfortunately we are not aware that we have

The prince placed the cup of tea on the table and sat up.

“I know the difficulty,” he replied with a smile, “of winning the
affections of these two children, the three-thousand or so. That is why
I wish to meet Mortemart and Morio, the leaders of the fortune of
these two. Perhaps you are already acquainted with the former. But
will you give us a brief account of the latter?”

Anna Pávlovna’s face flushed and softened.

“Morio is the greatest of our modern French philosophers,” she said
as she decided to speak earnestly.

“As I am sure,” said the prince, entering into conversation, “that
Morio is such a great man, I believe you should know him a little
more, and you will do me a great favor if you do so.”

Anna Pávlovna took a seat on the sofa near the prince’s.

“Of course,” she replied, “I know him well. I have been to him many
times.”

“I have,” said the prince, lowering his head to share in this
act of intimacy. “Can you tell me something about him, please? I
am curious.”

“What you want to know is not surprising. But here is a problem: he
is a great thinker, and at the same time a great philanthropist, but
it seems to me that he has a certain morality, such as Montesquieu
would have understood, a morality founded on the profoundest
philosophy and on the best social ideas of the time.”

“I am always surprised,” said the prince, “that no one has come to
England to study his works. He has written a multitude of volumes.”

“I know it. I learned the whole of them in France. The only difference
I have is that I have never had the opportunity of seeing him. But
he has been my friend and his works are invaluable to me. Maybe I will
see him soon. But we have not the slightest acquaintance.”

“Who is it who will not go to England? Foresa is not going to
London, but where is it going?” asked the prince, who had a gift of
seizing everything that might be of use to him.

“The last European congress,” said Anna Pávlovna, interrupting him
by way of laughing and playfully rebuking him, “is the only one in
which we can take part. But present in England now is the general
Averoch, who is also to come here, and who will do me some favors. I
don’t know what to do about it.”

“I think it will be very useful,” said the prince.

“Do you for certain?” asked the woman.

“Certainly.”

“That was what I wanted to ask you. How, then, will you account for
your having first a ship then nothing?”

“Nothing? I don’t understand,” said the prince in a contemptuous
tone.

“How did you keep the ship?” was the only question she asked.

“I kept what?” replied the prince, embarrassed to change the subject
of conversation.

“What did you declare Monsieur de Lévis, who had money enough,
to do with it?” said the woman.

“I declare nothing,” said the prince.

“Then I declare nothing myself, and it was no longer money. What
were you keeping?”

“Children,” said the prince, ending the conversation with this one
question.

“Children?” repeated the woman, with a smile of profound and measured
fascination.

“Échard!” said the prince as he walked over to the windows to look
out, and then turned around. “Marx!” said he again; then, glancing
at the woman, “against Fournier!” said he in the utmost seriousness.

“As for me, I,” said the woman, with an affected sigh and a
tears-in-the-eye look, “have no other means to furnish my
household, than the legacy of M. de Lévis.”

The prince, who never failed to assume the attitude of a man of
learning, pondered this question in his mind. But his way of thinking
was more like that of a servant, and he answered only one question,
and this when he caught sight of the woman, in order to show, if
possible, that he had what she expected.

“I know the proverb to the letter: ‘A man who knows the
Proverbs has two hundred francs to spare.’”

“Well, then,” said the woman, “if you are not going to keep children
at home, what are you doing here?”

“I want to know you,” said the man.

“I want to know you,” repeated the woman, looking at the prince in
the face.

“Don’t play Mrs. Dryden,” said the prince, and then added: “I don’t
need to see you, this evening.”

“Good-by, dear Friend,” said the woman, whom he had just once
asked to be his luckless confidante.

**VIII.**

It rained in London, but the public fondly anticipated the arrival of
the Emperor. The great banquets on both sides went on, and the
Emperor, as all expected, had relaxed his previous promptitude and had
reposed himself in his state.

There were three or four reasons given by the Emperor in his own
favor, which were not to be considered in the present connection. The
chief of these was the fact that the Emperor had always been a
friend of the Court of England, even though he had sometimes been in
confrontation with it. But this reason was not enough to explain the
great devotion the Emperor showed to the English. He had always
hoped that the British people would think of their country’s
sufferings to the last and would never permit its government to
purposely injure the person of the Emperor of Russia. Still he had
hope that the British government would not fail to act in a manner to
bring this result. He had also hoped that England, in those
circumstances, would take the steps which all destiny had predicted.
The Emperor was perfectly sure that he could not take these steps
herself.

It was a rainy and cold spring day in 1806. In London there was a mass
of people regarding the arrival of the Emperor—all the people who
had any interest in the news, whether it were because they were
sponsors of the Emperor or because it was of interest to them in some
other way. The foreign section of the Court came to the gallows-door
at the palace, attended by the leading members of the household and
the Court officers, and the imperial soldiers also came and stood
in the street, with their arms crossed on each other’s shoulders.

Here they stood, in fact, in a gallery, and here they stood to
refuse entry to one who did not come accredited.

The Emperor’s carriage was drawn by twelve or fourteen merino
horses, and was like a metal object that was to be seen in the
Pasquillí of Hatschek’s paintings, with a detached carriage of the
same style. It was a heavy carriage, and because of this it was drawn
by several horses.

As the carriage entered the square, the doors of the gallows-door
were opened, and the Emperor was first seen, standing below the
dome, a translucent green cloak unbuttoned to the neck, and a fine,
silvered hat, which showed the shine of his bald head. He stood
gazing into the sky, and then he threw himself on his hands in the
parking ground, and there made his entrance.

Everyone was astonished and greatly pleased, but most of all the
soldiers. This last group of people was probably the most interested
in the whole spectacle, for the Emperor had been very fond of them
during the last year or so, and on his arrival in London they
demonstrated a great loyalty and adoration.

But this did not last. The Emperor himself was gravely dressed, and
his first clothes had been on his return from St. Petersburg. He was
with us in the people’s costume, but he had been wearing a military
uniform when he came to London.

The officers and the men had once more stood before him, but a few of
them, who were of importance, had retired to the gallery. The
soldiers were at last sent away to their quarters, and the imperial
soldiers themselves went to the bank of the Thames to take the
prayers which the Emperor had made to the Sovereign of the People in
St. Petersburg, and to jeer at the English and at the French.

Here he made a speech of which the officers and men only heard when
it was translated into the soldiers’ dialect. He spoke in very simple
German and his face was flushed from the heat and passion of his
speech. He had the same fervor with which an Indian captain of a
prison deserter would have spoken to the Indian captors of his
capture. The emotion had been so great that the Emperor, though he
was a tall, dark, and resolute man, had a slight trembling in his
features and the color of his face was red through the thick greasy
hair, in spite of the large quantity of hair that he had.

The English had come to London to see the Emperor, not to try to
move him. They had come to see the rest of the world’s Emperor. But
there was no one to see the rest of the world, and he had come to
London, whom he assumed to be the only one in Europe. He had not come
here to see the Court, and he would not have done it if he had wished
to. He had come to see the people. The people had come to see the
Emperor, and the Emperor had come to see them. But he wanted to see
something more. Everything in the world was before him, but he wanted
the thing that was most precious. He spoke with the passionate
husbandry of an old man, who had learned to love; he spoke to the
English as to his young lovers. He had been in England only once,
but in England, and he had been the first Emperor to have been there.
He had spoken with them and I like to think that the Emperor could
not have spoken to them without being full of tenderness, because the
Emperor was a tender man. He had been with us for some days and he had
seen us—in fact, he had seen us. And he had seen us without becoming
Angelic, like the Emperor of Prussia, or without becoming grotesque,
like the Emperor of Austria. The Emperor had seen us in all our
weaknesses and he had been amused and touched by our misery, and he
had also had the understanding to know and to feel what was in us.
And then he had come to see the English.

The English were not of great length or height, and the Emperor had
not been long and happy in England. He was not beautiful, and he did
not care if he looked beautiful. He had been bad but he was a brave
man, and he was a man who had never wanted to be himself. He did not
need to be himself in order to be the Emperor of the whole world.
Accustomed to the world, he had learned to forget himself and to
keep his character. He had been a good and devoted man, and he was a
man who had lived many years, and he had enjoyed his life. He had
liked to play the part of a good man, and this was the part he had
deigned to be played in England and elsewhere. And so he saw us, and
he saw us. He saw us in all our misery and in the hope that he would
not always be able to help us. He saw us also in the light and the
darkness of an insane man, who wanted nothing for himself but the
good of his fellow-men, and he saw us also in the hope that we should
be able to give him something that he could not give himself. No
good could be given to him without the giving of some evil in return
—which was the only way in which the world could be saved. And
the Emperor wished to be the one man upon whom the world could rely.

“You are the Emperor of the world,” said he.

“It is not for me if you wish to establish a monarchy in one of
my provinces. I would like to know your opinion on the matter.”

“You are the Emperor of the world,” said the English.

“Anything you like,” said the Emperor. “And do you not pray to the
Emperor of Heaven?”

“Of course,” said the English.

“Is it not time for you to abandon all that you are doing now?
Passions and petty policies are destroying you, and you ought to
think of the Emperor who holds the key of the world.”

“You are the Emperor of the world,” said the English.

“Do you not pray?” demanded the Emperor.

“Of course I pray.”

“Do you not pray to the Emperor of Heaven?” said the Emperor.

“Of course I do.”

“Does he desire that you should abandon all that you are doing now?”

“I do not see how you can change me,” said the English.

The Emperor had no difficulty in coming to the conclusion that the
Emperor of Heaven was not going to change his man. He had not looked
upon this so long as he had been the Emperor of Prussia, and he was
not likely to be now. The Emperor, knowing the nature of men, knew
that there is no one who can make a man. There is only one thing by
which a man can be made: he will make his fortune and his name.
There is another way: he will make his country and he will have the
favor of an Emperor. So the Emperor wanted to show that he could
make his country. He saw the English in this country; he saw them
with his own eyes, and he saw them in all their misery, for which
they had to forgive him. And he went on in his way. He said that he
did not know the British constitution, but he knew that if the
English and the French could not agree, they could not be saved.

“Nor Russia,” said he, “will save the world if it does not agree
with me.”

“Nor Austria,” said the English, “nor Prussia.”

“No! of course not!” said the Emperor.

“Nor England?”

“No! of course not!” said the Emperor.

“Nor your own people?”

“No! of course not!” said the Emperor, some pain in his voice.

“I am the Emperor of the world,” said he; “and if Russia does not
agree with me, the world will go to the Emperor of Heaven.”

The Emperor was in the palace and in the street now, and he was going
out to wait for the guests. He was going out to wait for the barons,
the baronets, the baronesses, and the barones, and all the
opponents of the Emperor.

The people had many things to do, but they wished to go to the
Emperor. He was the only one to whom they could go unreservedly.

The Emperor entered his carriage, and he went out into the
streets. The sun was shining, and the great bodies of the people were
running out from the town, and the Emperor was not slow in
appreciating their haste. And he walked over to the gallows-door,
where the men and the officers of the Court were standing, and he
said to them: “Bring your ladies. I want to look at them.”

And he went up to the gallows-door, where he could get a good
view of the ladies, and in front of him the outriders stood with their
arms crossed on each other’s shoulders.

The Emperor entered the gallows-door and stood among the
outriders, and he said:

“Do you know my way in the Court? From where I come, I know all the
paths.”

The men of the household made ready for him, and he entered.

Here were the King of the Netherlands, the King of Naples, and the
king of Portugal, and the Duchess of Sardinia.

The Emperor was not surprised to find them. He was glad enough to
meet them, but he did not express his pleasure. He was not a showy
personality, and he would not in any way be presented to the Court.
He had a great bad feeling toward the Court, and he would not say
anything about the Court. But he had not had time to think
throughfully on this matter, and the feeling was not present, and he
really did not like people talking about themselves.

The Emperor then passed from the gallows-door to the gallery, and he
stood there to address the Court. He spoke as the people had spoken to
him and listened to, and as the people had spoken to him and had
expected him to speak to.

“The Court of Europe,” said he, “has been the most wonderful
experience of my life. In the court of Europe, I have seen how
humblest of people, when they have made a vocation, are able to find
the greatest activity. The court of Europe is a school where the
uxuality of the heart and the depth of the studies of the soul are
most greatly developed. I have seen the greatest of all the

The prince, who had often been the subject of such tender
remarks—more often than any of his contemporaries—gave a dispassionate
gratification of the eyes. Anna Pávlovna saw that he felt her
expressions, and she avoided him as if seeing a bridge to be
crossed.

“But Anatole,” she said with color in her cheeks, “it is true you
have put a lot of effort into his education. I know you have said to
that very charming lady with whom he was engaged that you would do
everything for him.”

The prince’s eyes fell into his hands. For the first time he uttered a
confiding and impetuous voice.

“I only wish Anatole would be a scholar,” said he.

“Ah! No, I know you have a great talent for teaching. I don’t
believe he is only a scholar, but he has a great memory. And he had the
choice of his teacher, a most excellent chemist, the most clever man I
have ever seen. The academic methods are very detrimental. But, let
alone Anatole! I never knew anyone with a better memory. Your son
must be one of the brightest sons of the Empire.”

The smile on the prince’s face closed suddenly. He had not been
smiling in his entire life, never smiling at anything, but had always
been coldly impassive.

“You are quite right,” said he. “I would not have been able to make
him better had I not chosen him wisely. But I don’t think Anatole will
make good work. I don’t believe he has the talent.... He is an idealist;
he doesn’t learn easily, and he lacks explanation. He doesn’t understand
the world, and he is a very lazy child. He would only be good to
signalize his greatness by the number of pitfalls he would have found
in the world, and then be pejorative and brutally vulgar in the
description. I don’t believe he will ever reach the top. He never
understands anything. He seems to have been condemned to learn
nothing.”

“I don’t believe him,” said the prince. “It is a worthy
character.”

The prince’s expression was one of deep and abiding conviction. For
the first time he had noticed the disparity between the words of
Anna Pávlovna and the realities of life and the depths of the truth
which she had exposed. He had been a man of superficial delicacy, who,
in the company of those of his own age and rank, was always thinking of
flattering people and others, and in his own private life he was a
clumsy and irritating person, who was continually trying to make others
impress him. But now, in the presence of Anna Pávlovna, who had
revealed to him the secret of his own soul and had thrown light on his
most secret thoughts, he had felt in his heart the obligations
invited by the greatness of the native girl.

Anna Pávlovna, as she spoke, was leaning forward and almost
touching her hand towards the prince with her golden-colored fingers.

“Tell me,” she said, “do you love Anatole?”

“Do you love him, I ask you? Do you love all the children
I’ve given you? Your father has loved them as well as I have loved them.
Can you be any different? And am I any different? Do you want me to
love him? I don’t believe you want him, but I am now asked to do so.
Ask yourself, do you wish to be the mother of a beautiful and
dignified child? If you are the mother of an addict to power who is
obstinate in the same mistakes as his father, you don’t wish to be
mother. You are not there because your father is a fool, but because he
makes you a mother, and one that only he knows. You love him. But if
he himself doesn’t love his children, can you?... I say this because
I know you love your son, even though he has no feeling. But I don’t
know if he loves you as you know he does. You don’t want your son
healthy and happy. He has no appetite, he makes a fool of himself,
and he feels nothing. You don’t want him to enjoy what your mother
gives him. He has no true affection for you. But I saw you come home
with Anatole in arms, and you came angry and angry, not finding him at
all. You were happy to see him at school, not caring him a whit. You
don’t want to raise him. You now find that he will not become a good
soldier, and therefore you resent him and he has to carry your
hate on his shoulders.... We can’t help it. We are not all like you.
You have a passionate nature, but you don’t realize it. I know you
don’t love Anatole. No one ever does. But you believe that you love
your son. All women believe this. But what do you wish to do with Anatole
and him? You wish to marry him? You are young to be a wife, but your
children are already old enough to be husbands and fathers. Now I
explain the tortures of an old marriage. Do you see that? You are not
a happy wife, and Anatole does not know it. He thinks you are his
perfect mistress. He has been afraid all his life, and now he thinks
he is a man and has been chosen for his station and life. He says he
will always be your faithful slave, and that you will always have
him, and that he will be your whole life. You look on him as a
slavery, and you enjoy it. You don’t know it yourself, but you are
happy in the knowledge that you will always have the presence of a
slave, and you will have him around the clock, but he will never learn
to be a free man. You say that Anatole has the spirit of a hero who
will sacrifice himself in war. Do you think this is true? You say
his voice is clear. Well, he has the voice of an idiot. He never speaks
for himself, and never expresses either his own feelings or own
opinions. He does not speak. He never himself desires and declares.
He comes to you with your whim, he is your genius. Do you realize that
he is making fools of you? Do you know that with him your life is a
monotonous stage of misery? I don’t know if you could endure it
longer. When I saw the poor Anatole, I saw that he was not a man, but a
crazy invalid. I wish you to have children with him. And so you are
called to be a mother, believing that he will give you the strength
and the will that your family, your country, and your happiness
require. But I can’t tell you the truth, you can’t tell me the truth.
You are in love with him, and love is not a man’s profession. He
thinks you are a good mother, but you are not, and what you are is
nothing for Anatole. He sees only your cruelty. And what of you?...
You are nothing, and nothing will save you. You are a poor woman.
And what about Lord Hope? You think like an old woman, and nothing
more. You are the lover of a madman, and you are the wife of the
fool. You want to marry him. What have you in return, only a family,
which you don’t want to keep, and to which you don’t wish to devote
yourself?... Well, let us not talk more about this topic. I want to
know something more about you. Have you been to the military?
Recently? Listen! Is it really true you have been to the military?
You ought to have been to the military! The only place to find true
men, men who will stand up for themselves, men who will deliver
territory and land, men who will fight for the glory of their
country. Marshal Künkel, the last of the great French generals,
without him you would have given up all your attempts to make
Europe understand the Emperor Alexander. But the Emperor Alexander
would not have done anything without Marshal Künkel. He would not
have saved us without him. And I can’t believe that you are going to
make friends with that disfigurement and that spiritual weakness and
that intellectual powerlessness. You are nothing but a woman. And
with what are you going to make friends?... Your beauty will not save
you. And that’s all you have to say about it. I’m sorry to say it,
but I don’t believe you have any feeling. I want to know if you are
deeply moved, and I don’t believe you are. You are a mean,
frivolous, and weak woman. You don’t speak. You don’t understand the
meaning of your own life. You don’t realize that you are not a
woman, but an invalid. You are not a man. You are nothing. And what
will be the result? I don’t know. But I don’t hope anything good, and
only a complaint and bitter murmurs of being an invalid. I don’t
know whether anybody will care to listen to you.... I say this, not in
a sad tone, but I feel that you are not well, and that you are not a
woman who would not remain silent about this. You are not a man, and
I don’t know whether it is better for you to be a woman and a
brute.... I’ve said a lot, and I hope you won’t say anything, and I
don’t want you to say anything. I haven’t been seen very often by the
Dowager Empress. We have not had any conversation, and this is bad. If
I had known you were ill at the English arrival, I would not have
come here. But I’ve said you were well, and I said that you were going
to the English arrival. Now I’m not saying that you went to the
English arrival. I’m saying that you were well. I am not saying that
you were ill at the English arrival. I’m speaking of two different
times. I haven’t seen you at the English fete, and that’s why you’re
here. You told me you were ill when you left St. Petersburg, but now
you say you were well. You said you were going to the English arrival
because you were ill, but you went to the English arrival because you
were well. I’ve said it a lot. I’ve spoken to you about it. I want you

But you have two very nice children and no one has ever been sure if

she attend the schools? She is not well enough to do so. If there were
an army here to welcome her, she would take it to the brim.”

“Why do you say that, your Eminence?”

“Because I know her and I know you well,” she replied with a cold
and reproaching look.

“Ah! that was enough to draw me to the top of my fancy. The
Empress will do as she pleases. The Germans will do as they please. I
will do as I like: I will cast out the children I do not like. I will
say no more about her. I shall try to say nothing about you.”

“For me, indeed, woman, there is nothing to be done. You must say
no more about me and you will say nothing, and so I know myself in who
I am.”

“You are sure?” said Anna Pávlovna, her eyes blazing with anger. She
looked at the prince, who had not yet moved his foot. She was too
tantrally temperamental to be forced out of it.

“Then you have thrown me out altogether,” she said in an assumed
voice, and turned to the door. She sat down again and laughed harshly,
opening the door, and throwing her head back as if she were going to
swallow a bitter pill.

The prince said nothing, only slightly shocked and hurried to take
teas in the servant’s room, which was hitherto untouched by the
entourage. Then the servant returned and asked the way to the
chamber. Anna Pávlovna said that she was not ready to have anything
to do with anyone and she had taken tea in the servant’s room. The
prince followed her and listened to her outburst.

“Vienna!” she began abruptly. “My dear! You do not know what you
are saying. I mean, that the Emperor Alexander will crush Virginius
to the ground. He will crush him to pieces! That’s the only thing I
can say. They are trying to deceive us. You are trying to deceive us!
You are trying to deceive our good and virtuous sovereign! She is
saving us, not the other way round! She will crush the hydra to the
ground! You—you—you are trying to deceive us, and you are deceiving
yourself! You think you are doing something for us, but you are only
hurting us to the core! Violence and delay are the best antidotes to
revolution. This is how they must be stopped! You would have sent
Tatarinov to us! You would have sent Zwingenich, and I know that the
baron. Could Balz have sent him? And you, with all your sense, your
culture, your beauty, your eloquence, have never said anything for
the people in your country and you have spoken only for yourselves.

“Grandfather, that is unnecessary,” replied the prince.

“But you, I think, do not wish so much for yourself. No, no: I
think you wish for your children. Now that you have got two splendid
children, it is all easy for you. And what are we to say of the others?
We can only say that you are free and happy. You have nobody to love
but your children, and you are so possessed by them that you are
contented and happy. Well, let it be so. You are happy. Do you
think, too, that there are no such things as insane people? No,
there are some who never understand life, and always cannot get
out of the pit into which they have been thrown. Do you know what I
mean by this? You have your wife, whom I know perfectly well, and she
is not an insane person, nor has she been; nor is her husband. But
there are some of your friends who have perished by their own fault,
not by the fault of the Emperor, or any one else, but by their own
mischief and violence. It is they who cannot get out of the pit, and
the Emperor himself is chief of the pit. He has entered it and cannot
give them out. And of all those who are in the pit some are mad. You
don’t know what an idiot Manstein was. (Manstein’s last name is
pronounced ‘Mansien.’) You know nothing about a madman. A madman is
only an idiot who understands nothing. A madman is a man who cannot
get out. I do not know what to say about him. I have told him about
him, but he does not listen, and when I have gone the first night he
has gone off in a rage. One night before I went to the grand fete I went
to him, and he said to me: ‘I don’t believe in you, you don’t talk
any more about the Emperor than you do about her! I don’t believe you
are going to do anything for me any more.’ I said I would, but he
would not believe I was going to do anything for him, and could not
understand what it was I was going to do. He said: ‘I will never do
any more anything for you,’ and he went off. What am I to say to him?
I could not understand him and did not understand him. You know the
thing about idiots. And you, you have no friends any more. Is there
any one whom you consider a true friend? No. But for the most part
you are not your own friend; you do not know whether you love your
children or not; you know only what you see, and generally you are
not even your own friend. You have done nothing for the past four
years, and you are content. But you are not content. You are sometimes
deeply moved, but you do not know how to console yourself or anyone
else. And after all you will not find any consolation in the world.
As for the Dowager Empress, I am sure you do not care for her.”

The prince did not wish to argue, but only asked whether the baron
was well.

“Of course. She too is ill,” said Anna Pávlovna. She fell into a
drowsy reverie, and, penetrating into the depths of this reverie,
finally said:

“Oh, I am quite well now,” as she wrote the page she meant to address
to her son. She went on to say that the baron’s indisposition was of an
acute kind and caused him to be constantly ill.

“Ah!” said the prince, in a tone of curiosity, “what is the
baron doing?”

“Nothing. He is lying about a very dangerous fever.... I don’t know
whether to believe him or not. He is a very dirty person. I am sure he
will die, but only after all that has happened. You will hear about
it,” she added. “The Emperor will have to listen to the baron!”

“In any case,” said the prince, “we cannot go down to Lucca. I have
heard that when your battery is ready we cannot leave it here, but we
must go. I am going to England at the beginning of August.”

“I have been thinking of Lucca,” said Anna Pávlovna, a little
astonished. “It is a very beautiful town and filled with antiquities.
I will go down there, and then I will write to you.”

She said this with great tenderness, and she was right. She was not
able to write anything to her son. She was not even able to write to her
friend the baron, who, though captive and only sixteen, was now the
most popular man in the world. Madame de Montemart was a great
friend of the Empress’s, and an admirable poet. She was not even able
to write to him, the eldest of whom, the marquis, had died in October,
1804.

“Ah, my dear friend,” she said as she put the document into her
head, “I have written to him.”

“I wrote.”

“Certainly, yes, but I wrote this: ‘I have not had the pleasure of
seeing you, and I am exceedingly sorry, still more, as I have not
reached you—’ and I was to say: ‘I am in the grand fete at the
English ambassador’s and I am rejoiced to have you join me, for we
ought to spend the evening together.’ I wrote that altogether. But in
retrospect I see how the piece has fallen to the ground.”

The prince had been about to go to the English ambassador’s that
morning. But what did it matter? He could not go. His first
obligation was that of the Emperor, which he must have satisfied.
However, he must have been visited by the Empress Márya Fëdorovna
and by the baron, who would have wished him to take an interest in
them.

“Well,” said the prince to himself, “but about Novosíltsev he is to
be hanged in three days’ time; it is a good sort of sentence.”

He waved the piece over to the baron; and the baron’s face was full
of a sort of emotion, which seemed to him of a very peculiar and odd
kind. He lifted the piece and said:

“I am obliged to you. I can die without being hanged.”

Anna Pávlovna read the note as she handed it to the baron, and she
gave him the Emperor’s advice for her son.

“I wished you to have a good look at the baron, Madame,” said the
baron, as he turned to leave.

“Ahh! That is enough! This is no place for your friends. The baron
can come here later. You will see him. And you will see the Colonel
and Colonel Bacowski, and you will see the baron’s wife young
Flora, and she will show you an exact copy of a picture of her
mother.”

Anna Pávlovna paused while the baron went off, and she resumed:

“You know, the Emperor has decided that the Dowager Empress must
immediately be invited to St. Petersburg, and that is immovable. The
Dowager Empress will have to come. Your Majesty is obliged to
dispatch for the bailiff to Lucca.”

The Prince had said nothing for three minutes; he did not look at her
and he did not answer, but there was no question in his mind. Then he
suddenly asked:

“What do you mean by saying ‘imovable’?”

“What do you mean?”

“Then you will be obliged to go to Lucca?”

“Of course. I will go down there.”

“You will go?”

“Yes,” said the prince, with something of a smile.

At this moment the baron entered, and Anna Pávlovna said, with a
well-brought-up and courtierlike pity:

“I wrote to him that you would take an interest in my son. What
would you do? You know nothing about him. And I told him that he
must have a look at the baron....”

The baron stepped forward and, without looking at Anna Pávlovna,
said:

“I will go to Lucca to do what I can here.”

“I thought you would say something about Novosíltsev. Go now and
tell him I wish you good luck, and let him know that I fear he will
die.”

The baron turned round and said:

“I am going quickly to Lucca.”

The baron went off, and the prince hesitated a moment.

“Do you really think me wayward?” said he to himself; and then he said
to himself:

“You will leave Lucca? You will take Novosíltsev to Lucca? You will
dare to go down there? You did not think I would go to Lucca either!
And what did you think of the baron?” But he said nothing.

‘How am I to do it? Will I go down to Lucca and bring the baron’s
wife back to me?’ he asked himself. ‘And will I go down there with
Novosíltsev?’

He did not know whether he should go or not; and then he answered
himself:

“I must go down to Lucca to see Novosíltsev.”

He would have been able to say more, but he stopped himself. There
followed a silence which he had not known until he came to it. Then he
said:

“I will go down there. Some time ago I wished to go down there; but
now I will go down there.”

He went to the window and looked over at the palace.

‘Pray, why went down to Lucca?’ he asked himself.

‘I had some things to do there. I had to go down to Lucca to see
Novosíltsev. And now you say, “I have to go down to Lucca.” What
difference shall we make? I had to do something here, and now I am
going down to Lucca to see Novosíltsev. And the baron, who is also
going down to Lucca, will go to Lucca; or will he stay in Lucca? Ah!
this is all nonsense! I have to go down to Lucca for Novosíltsev, and
the baron will go down there; or will the baron stay in Lucca?’

‘I must go down to Lucca,’ he said to himself, and added:
‘But what will the baron do? I will go down to Lucca and bring the
baron’s wife back to me. What a fun!’

At this he went up to Anna Pávlovna.

“Who shall I tell about this?” he asked.

“If you don’t know what I mean it will do you no good,” she said
with a smile and a sigh of blame.

“I will go down to Lucca, and as for the baron, farewell! He can do
whatever he likes.”

The Prince went down to Lucca, where he found Novosíltsev waiting for
him. He asked him to come to him, and he quietly went back to the
Palace of the Grand Dukes, where he met the baron, whom he found
already seated.

“Would you like tea? I have brought you a cup,” said the Prince
passing the chambermaid the cup and saucer to the baron, who accepted
them.

“No thank you. I can do no such thing. Coffee is better than this
tea; and you can’t give me a cup of it either.”

Then he asked the Emperor’s advice, and moreover he asked the
Emperor’s advice about Novosíltsev.

“I’m quite sure,” said the Emperor, “that you will not do me any
harm. A hangman who does not want to be executed will hang himself,
or become mad. It’s the Emperor’s policy that the hangman shall have
at least a certain control of his own affairs, and so he will go
down to Lucca so that he can be sure of his own power. Where do you
know him best? I’m sure you know him better than anyone else. And
after all, we are all at your mercy. You are the first to do things
you consider wrong, and those who follow you are not responsible for
them.”

The Emperor was a powerful and strong man, and had a clear and
sharp manner of speaking. He was interminable in conversation, but the
Prince had not heard him for some time.

“Not that I don’t wish to see the baron; but I don’t wish to see him
now. I wish you came here, so that I could write to you. I wish you
could go down to Lucca, and say things to him, and bring back to him
what you can, and leave him to come here. I will come down to Lucca
and say things to the baron, and I will not write any more about this
to you. I will do what I can, and now I wish you would come down to
Lucca and say something to the baron, and leave me to write to you
and do what you can. I’m sure he will go down to Lucca to meet you,
and then you will know what to do.”

How would this be possible? What would he say to the baron, if
Novosíltsev did not go down to Lucca himself?

He said to himself:

“He’ll go down to Lucca, but we know nothing about the baron.
What can we do? What can we do? I wish I could write to the baron
and say what I wish! But I don’t know what to write to the baron.
And I don’t know what to say to Novosíltsev! Do we really know
anything about the baron?”

He took the baron’s arm and began to talk to him of Novosíltsev, for
whose sake he had come to Lucca, and who had put him at the baron’s
disposal.

“But I wish I knew nothing about Novosíltsev!” he said to the
baron. “Well, I’ll tell the Emperor about him; and I’ll tell him
that you have said to me that you don’t know him and that you are
very attached to him, and that you want the Emperor to do him all the
good you can. But you don’t know anything about him. Your own first
step in your life was to take his side against the Duke of Yorck, for
you wanted to show your attachment and devotion. But now when you
have become a man you don’t know anything about him, and you are not
sure that he is what you wish him to be. I would like you to know him
better. Do you know him? Don’t you? And I would like you to tell me.
You know him; for you were not at a wedding. Well, I want you to know
him better, than we know anything about him; and I want you to
tell me what he is, and what you have said about him. Don’t you
understand that you want to say that you are his friend, and that you
wish to save him and all his friends? And I would like you to say all
this to Novosíltsev. But no, you don’t say anything. I don’t know
what to say to him, nor what to do. And there is nothing for me to
do, except go down to Lucca and see what I can do, except say
something to the baron. I would like him to say that he wishes to
save Novosíltsev, and to say that he is his friend; and then he can
go down to Lucca and bring his own son here.”

The Prince was quite tired. He did not want to talk any more. He was
not able to talk about anything. He had told the baron that he did
not wish to come down to Lucca with him, and then he went up to the
window.

‘If I knew it, I should go down to Lucca,’ he said to himself; and
then he went up to the Empress’s room.

The Empress Márya Fëdorovna had not gone to the baron’s; and she was
the only remaining member of the inner circle of the Court. She
suggested that the Prince should go to the baron, and the baron
should go to the Prince.

‘Who is this he?’ thought the Prince, going upstairs to the Empress’s
room. ‘What has become of this man?’

The world loves the heroes of the past and the present and speaks

“But how do we do?”

“Let us make a review, and wherever the people do it, we do it, and

A few days later the Grand Consul came and asked what had become of
the German ambassador, who wanted to get him back into the Cabinet
of State.

“Perhaps he will come in away or say that he does not wish to come
in any more,” the Grand Consul replied to the servant, as the man
was coming in, and instead of maintaining himself upon the salary of
the foreign minister, he decided to devote himself to the commerce
of the commerce. He was not a man of nervous energy and vigor, but
he was a solid actor; he did his very complete job, the very smart
job. He was not a man of his age; he had been able only to differ from
the average man, to be one of the active men who distinguish themselves
by their own powers rather than by their gift, and was a great friend
of the Emperor Alexander, who had spoken often, condemned him, but
had never denied him even when he was not working in a circle of his
own choosing, always offering him a favorable disposition in his
thoughts.

Once he spoke to the Empress Márya, whom he described as a good
woman, and said that he felt that the Empress was needing him. It was
said that on one occasion little Empress Márya was supposed to have said
to him: “My dear friend, one of my father’s plums comes to me from
the Emperor,” and she meant the Emperor Alexander. But he spoke
against her judgment and therefore did not believe that what she said
was true. He left the Empress acquainted with the friendship of his
own, which was imponderable. He was not the least man of honor in
the service of the Emperor Alexander, and he knew how to put his own
before the Emperor. He was, on the contrary, always easily deceived by
the Emperor in far-away places and in great matters. He was always at
the comfortable end of the Emperor Alexander’s patience and never
reached the point where he could say, as he did at the time of
Napoleon’s verbal rejection of his ideas about creating heaven on
earth: “I want to be Napoleon of Europe, and I am only better skilled
at this. I am the Emperor Alexander of England!” In his own good
senses he never hardened into the Emperor Alexander’s accuser; but he
was on the other hand a man who has never erred in any matter. He
always approached things from the most safe point of view. Never did
he err from the inevitability of things, nor did he err from any
subject. He merely deviated from everybody else from his point of
view. He was always on the side of what he thought right, that is, of
what he thought to be the interests of the Emperor Alexander, and
therefore left it always to his own wish and judgment. He was one of the
best protégés of the Emperor Alexander, and an interregnum (that is,
a solemn but conducive interpretation by the Emperor Alexander) was
the Empire of the Emperor Alexander. He never missed opportunity to
come forward and make himself precious to the Emperor Alexander. He
was always prepared for anything and committed himself to it. And no
report ever made him look sly or inclined to cowardice. He was a man of
noble character and of great success. He was always happy, even though
he did not, and did not wish to, do the Emperor Alexander anything
wrong; and the Emperor Alexander did not hurt him. He knew nothing of
the Emperor Alexander’s thoughts, and only went into them when he
heard them. He was certain of the Emperor Alexander’s principles and
not at all of his opinions. His conviction of these principles was
exactly the same whatever the views entertained by the Emperor
Alexander. He was not a party man, but he made himself a disinterested
philosopher, and this made him the friend of the most powerful men.
Never did the Emperor Alexander find himself in the unpleasant position
of an enemy of anyone. He was always able to say, “My friend has
done me a great service!” It was a philosophically correct idea that
for a man to be the friend of the Emperor Alexander meant that he
believed in the Emperor Alexander and was not the Emperor Alexander’s
enemy. This was the principle of the Empress and was the principle of
the world; she loved it, and it continued to prevail in the world.
But Napoleon was the worst enemy of all the ideas which had arisen in
the last years of the eighteeneenth century. She was the only idea
that could have made a man the Emperor Alexander’s friend. Napoleon
died in 1821. Herder, the greatest of takers of bribes, and who
lives in secret, left a will in which he gave, as he said, “a great
fortune” to the Emperor Alexander and “nothing” to others.”
Literature was the only legitimate thing in the universe. Napoleon
knew that and wanted to make all other parties believe that he did
not. He was a man without moral qualities; an insolvent, merciless

on the contrary, was the soul of a people, and at the age of forty
he became a man of heaven. He is the greatest man in the world in
spirit and in energy. He is always full of thoughts and ideas, but he
never thinks any other way than setting them down in an orderly
sequence. It is not only his strength that cannot be used, but his
impotence enough to stand any obstacle. He is a perfect man. As for
himself, he is the only man whose one-sidedness was endless. He was
praising him when he praised him, and he always put the slip when he
doubted him. He believed no one, but he was perfectly innocent. He
was contented with nothingness. He is the unlucky man. He is fast, but
not monstrous; he is the Hercules of the world. Nothing can stop
him; he is the great one, and very much more. But he did not like to
be evil, and he did not make himself good either. Emperor Napoleon,
on the contrary, was an immovable force; he was the disaster maker

In 1805 the French had invaded Portugal; the remnants of his army
had evacuated Ceuta, and had even penetrated as far as the city of
Lisbon, which was garrisoned only by a few hundred French troops.
Ménard’s French army was a garricoated army, that is, an army of
exhausted and rather sapped men. It spent but a few days in the
presented town of Ceuta, which was now under siege, and consequently
gave up a poor garrison. Its resources were not sufficient to maintain
an army of that number daily; and it was ordered to abandon it.
Consequently, some French officers and soldiers, tired of such a
careful waiting, turned to the entire Egyptian army. The Egyptians
believed that the French were going to warm it up and do battle.
They would take the squares with the garrisons, so that if they found
some new resistance without reaching the suburbs of Ceuta the
garrison would have to be evacuated with the garrisons and the
defence of the city would be weakened. But Napoleon was not going to
hold some city ports against rotten soldiers, and he left the
garrisons there. He did not want to hold up the first French army of
the century, the one from 1813, that pushed down the Russians, and
Coligny orders the evacuation of Ceuta, the tenth of October.

The British, who had in 1804 captured Toulon, had left fifty
thousand soldiers in the port to the garrison. But they did not
leave the soldiers. Napoleon ordered the evacuation of the French
troops from Toulon, and the British, by only a few orders, hastened
the evacuation of the nearby port of Marseille, where there were sixty
thousand soldiers. Napoleon knew that all his forces were now
extremely weakened, and he did not attempt to cross the Strait of
Mediterranean. The Anglo-French forces sailed away from there.

But the Great Armistice was early made. The Emperor Alexander had
already decided that he wanted an armistice with the English, but
that he would only agree to peace if neither the English nor the
French did anything that was not absolutely necessary, and if the
soldiers were ordered to return to port as soon as possible. All the
troops in the northern and eastern provinces were to begin returning
on the first of August. But there were already so few soldiers left in
the delta that the Emperor Alexander did not wish to oppose the
English. And though a direct movement from the north was intended to
provoke the English into making peace, yet the British could have
done nothing since Napoleon’s troops were still active and had the
enemy’s confidence. Napoleon succeeded in arranging the armistice
only by back and forth movements of the English and of the French
troops. ***(Footnote 60: See the chapter on the Great Armistice. This
armistice was made on 22 September 1805.)**

All this was coordinated by a plan drawn up by the French General
Martin: if the English immediately appeared in the Straits of
Mediterranean, the troops themselves, in this action, would be
entrenched on the island of Duero, and left to do nothing but fight
for a year. Then the English, according to this plan, should make a
legal peace, and leave the post of this island, leaving the French,
through the generosity of the commander of the army, to take it for
their own gain. If the English wished to make a legal peace, they
should also have the principle of the Peace of Tordesillas (1493),
which would constitute the dividing line between them and the
spoliation of the Europeans divided by the Cape of Guinea. It was
known that the Netherlands must be delivered over to the French,
and not the other way round; this would have tended to bring about a
military arrangement between England, France, and the Dutch Republic.
(The Dutch here actually had begun the war under the French; but they
were neutralized by the Treaty of Utrecht, and the English had
divided the Dutch territories, the one that could not be resented by
The Netherlands England France, and the Netherlands being in the
sense of this treaty, free from all military obligations to the
English, which is why the English did not accept the French terms of
the armistice.) All this was known to the Emperor Alexander, and he
did not wish to do anything. He wanted to arbitrate between England and
France and finally make the English give or accept the peace terms.

The English had been reinforced in their mainland troops (which
were back in the old greatholds of the islands of the northern
Ostrobothnian War) by fifteen thousand soldiers from the West
Indies. In addition to this, which was six thousand men, there were
three thousand soldiers, of whom half, as it was supposed that,
should have been designated for the service of this island. The
British, who intended to seize Duero, had ordered that thirty thousand
men should take the island, and that the sixteen thousand British
troops of the North Sea should be sent to this same point. But they
only brought with them two ships. These two ships sailed out of
Marseille; the king’s gun flat came to serve as a signal--the
Englishman was the first to do so and then the British small fleet
came up to the island in strength enough to compel its evacuation. The
commander in charge of the island was Mademoiselle d’Esparon (only
sixteen years old), who was an inexperienced woman, and with a fine
sort of Englishman, whose father had been a seaman and who had already
learned to captain his ship. They were waiting for the signal that
had to be made by the people there.

The English opened fire on the fortifications of the island in the
Txenturano bay. The French made a reply and then they retired entirely,
leaving the British, unmolested, to continue the attack and eventually
to capture the island. But the term of the armistice left this island
open for the French, since it was understood by both parties that the
only reason for the withdrawal of the French from Toulon and
Marseille was the necessity of withdrawing their troops from the
island. But the English made up their mind to hold on to the island,
and when they found the troops disorganized, surrendered the island.
And therefore the English did not make a peace.

All day long they spent at their leisure in their ship, but the
conscription force on the island was the constant enemy of their
inexperience (which made them go where they wanted to go). A thousand
men of the troops were killed by the French during the engagement,
the majority of whom had already been wounded. In all the attacks
deaths and wounded were upwards of two thousand--nor did the
military newspapers report that its own army was in a great state of
disorganization, so that there were two thousand soldiers missing.
Napoleon, counting the most violent and naked acts of English disregard
for the armistice, said that his hand was strong enough to do away
with the war with the English, and that the English and the English
would receive punishment.

The Emperor Alexander’s plan, as already mentioned, was to arrange
a truce between the English and the French and to reach an agreement
with the English. But the Emperor Alexander was too shrewd to know
that the English would make up their minds after the engagement to
get the island, and that he, in particular, was following the same
plan, that is, to arrange a truce between the English and the French
to make the English either give or accept an armistice, and to bring
about finally the peace, but also to do this without the necessary
military burdens to occupy the island (the most precise and necessary
condition which the Empire of France could not waive). This plan was
trivial and delicate in reality, but the Emperor Alexander was too
congenial and could not be all alone; he was obliged to make use of
the smallest means of his own power to finish the war with England.
At least this was the plan which even Napoleon himself had had in
mind; for all the facts that were known to him about what he considered
the obstacle to English occupation of the island and the arrangement
of a truce between the English and the French show that the plan
was even in the mind of Napoleon.

Napoleon proposed to wait for the British; but his plan was to
open a channel between the English and the French simultaneously. He
had intended that the English should not enter the Straits of
Mediterranean, but that they should have the English ship joined
with the inhabitants of the town of Sidra, in the territory of
Médéac, and should make an armada from this place against the
English in the Straits of Gibraltar to steam into the Mediterranean;
in this way the English should be blockaded, and on the other hand the
French, having had the arm of the English, should do battle against
them for one day, and then let the English go and occupy the island.
Before this arrival, however, Napoleon should break into a naval
passage from the island. If this were realized, the English would
be blockaded, the island would be occupied, and the name of peace
would remain in dispute. Now, what prevented the English from entering
the Straits of Gibraltar. That was another plan, one of which was
going to pass whatever methods were used to reach the end of this
blockade, or at least to prepare their transport vessels for
that.

But now the situation was completely changed. Both sides had taken
the island and had not accompaniment. And the English made that
garrison regulation which Napoleon had anticipated that the English
would make: **“le gauchage,” that is, leaving the garrison to
set to work, taking all the time since the evacuation of the island
was the time to strengthen, enlarge, and equip the garrison.**

So we began our march on Gibraltar, which the armies of the Great
and the Holy Roman Empire (which Napoleon had sent from Vienna)
arrived on only fifteen days ago. The French of the Mediterranean
annihilation division, under Marshal Mortemart, were now waiting for
the relief. On the bank of the Teber was an English army. But
externally, the Syrian army was stopped by the English. Napoleon was
keeping the enemy’s troop in quarantine, but Napoleon, in general,
thought nothing of this. The English were compelled to take a quiet
stand, for he thought that after the English would have to evacuate
the island immediately, and that the time was coming for the French to
enter. When the English had the latest dispatches, on the third day,
these were received: “I learned yesterday by a telegram from the
major of the post that the English army had arrived at the island and
unlimbered and quartermastered their artillery, but had never made
any attack.” This was the most worrying dispatch that could have
been received in three days.

        Disguise made it look like an accident. The Postmaster received
        the dispatch from the English with an English form that
        described the engagement, the French realizing that the
        English would leave the island immediately, and therefore
        rendering this dispatch no use.

The Emperor Alexander was called before the Grand Consul. He was not
the only one who had a plan and who knew it. All the admiral
Müellendorf and the noblese of the Greek League and the Grand
Consul himself knew it. They could have done nothing without knowing
it. It was a clearly drawn plan and was known to all. Napoleon and
the Emperor Alexander had it in mind, and they knew that they were
going to reach the end of the war only by this plan and only in view
of that plan. But this was not enough. The knowledge of that plan
could not make it so evident to all the world that the Emperor
Alexander and Napoleon had decided to do so, that not even a single
French person would have been convinced from the beginning of their
pursuit of the island, that he and Napoleon and the Emperor
Alexander were talking candidly of this plan and recognizing in the
enemies all the powers that ultimately should have been at the
ransom of it. All this was calculated to soften the opinion in the
world and to make the Emperor Alexander more moderate; and this was
the goal of all the conspiration, because the Emperor Alexander did
not want to do this for himself, but he could not, without the
knowledge of all this, let the world know in a sufficiently public
and impressive way that the Emperor Alexander was already partaking
with Napoleon in plans of this kind. The Emperor Alexander wanted only
to deceive, but the plan that he and Napoleon were going to propose
was well thought out and sound; the only obstacle was the
deceitfulness and artifice of the enemy; by deceiving the
eminent which the enemy did not understand he himself would deceive
itself. The Emperor Alexander wanted to deceive the world in his
own manner, even the Grand Consul and him were incorporated into the
drawings and the plans in the designs of friends and the head of
embassies, planning everything for this purpose. He made it so evident
to all people and peoples that he could not have done it otherwise.
After all this was known the Emperor Alexander used to say that
Napoleon, the most implacable liar and the best cryer of flattery,
did not even know that the Emperor Alexander had such a plan; but
this was not the case. But the plan that he and Napoleon were going
to do was so well thought out that no one could even imagine the way
that he and Napoleon could have discovered this either with one
person’s help or with two. Nobody understood it, and of course
Napoleon, who detested the Emperor Alexander, did not understand it
either, and he thought that this plan was ridiculous.

Napoleon wanted to seize the island and to take the field from the
British, and he had no other plan for it. He did not know that the
Empress was going to propose a truce with the English and make them
accept an armistice and leave the island. He did not know this either,
and only since the protection of the island now that he had left it
and ordered the march on it, it came to the knowledge of him. He was
going to enter the English on the island, and enter the city, and
win the battle in the most complete and simple way, going through
the assault on the barracks and French camp and taking it by
endurance. The Emperor Alexander was the greatest rival of the English
and the Turks, which empowered him to do anything and to do nothing;
but the Emperor Alexander could do more if he wished than everything
else in the world. He is quick and he is swift.

At the same time that the Emperor Alexander and Napoleon were
preparing this plan, the orders to the French were coming. Under
General Bagaut, they were reorganizing the army of the Mediterranean
Division, which was composed of small companies of pioneers. These
soldiers were dismounted and were under arms, and by the morning of
the twelfth day all the corps in the division were under arms,
except a few hundred. Among these there were corps of eight thousand
men. There were in the division that the common soldier, the
simplest of all the soldiers, and the soldier who was least in
demand, the war having only required heavy, civilized, and trained
soldiers; the countries in the provinces of the Mediterranean
Division had none of this. The common soldier was never seen in the
militia. They were in the ranks of the infantry, and there were only
two hundred able-bodied young soldiers among these eight thousand,
and the rest were merely men of all grades and ranks. They were
accustomed to service only in the field and only on honest work. But
now the information arrived that the British, who had received the
oath to do only unnecessary work, would have to leave the island,
and that indeed they had been in the island since they had
left Toulon, and that at the beginning they had only had a few
thousand men, but the Commander was in no hurry to do anything and
had twenty thousand troops in readiness, those being all the
troops of the garrison; those who had been in the island were not
all there at the moment of the British attack. The British had
disliked the enemy’s soldiers, who did not make the best impressions
on the terms of the armistice, and they expected to seize the
island from the French with their own army, and that if it failed they
would use the army of this island to come on the English. However,
the troops of the garrison were ordered by the English commanders to
set to work. This reduced the French division to a few hundred
soldiers. But Napoleon only sent the division from Marsey,
which, by the force of its own soldiers and regimental officers,
formed eight thousand men.

In reply to the Albanian Duke of Tresontz have you to me repeated
humanitarian, noted that the garrison defended itself with all the
savagery the English (the cannon which you sent to me in Constantinople
for the defense of the capital city and still standing) had not
faced in the same time, and that they were ready to take the field
and bring the English into a decisive fight. *To this, that of the
garrison disappeared from any report number a few hours.

At the same time that the complicated plan of the Emperor Alexander
and Napoleon was being difficult, the quartermaster in the court of
the Grand Consul’s home wrote the following message to the Grand
Consul on the third of the twenty-second: “On Saturday, the fortieth
day of August, the garrison opened fire on the English, and in the
morning of the ninth they left the island. The British that came
today are a very regular force and a very difficult enemy to
chase. If it is possible they may hunt a few soldiers, but the rest
will seek to come on you. If they come on you, we force, and these
troops will come on us by strong sounds and assume a false position.
In order that you may not have any trouble later and not have to
work hard, it appears that their force in the place of the garrison
is fifteen hundred men. If you have ten thousand men left, you will
have a strong march, but you know from them that you will easily
capture this place, and so we recommend you to take it at once.
After the capture, it will be necessary to have a plan for the
invasion of the island, and the deployment of the army in our
flank. But the enemy continues to stay in the island, and it is easy
to imagine. I want you to send me soldiers to join with the
diversions of the two [officers], and by the amount of time taken to
rise in time they will begin to work in the field. They will also work
at sea to find the English, and if they find them you will work to
block them.” *

In the morning the first person who received it was the ordinary
postmaster. The English had written to the language college in
Trebizond “that they wanted to reorganize the troops, which took
up ten thousand men,” and Napoleon had written to General Bagaut,

And the second copy of it was dispatched to the plain of
Lampouk. The General (Ardou) was preparing troops, but the field
comparably insufficient. Great Lirmouth, Lord of the Lirmouth
(11 794 square kilometers), is an important point of a great
importance. From it, as we propose, it will be necessary to take the
town of Lirmouth. If the town of Lirmouth falls into your hands,
then your army will pass through Lirmouth into the sea, and will
withdraw the English from Lirmouth. (This was not the plan of
Ménard after the conquest of Toulon. Frédéric, the Captain of the
French High Court of Justice, has in mind the conquest of Toulon.)
On the other hand, he says that after the conquest of Toulon, he
will put all the land units of Lirmouth in the hands of the
immediate commander, and send the French people to Lirmouth by ship.
This is the best plan, but why does the Duke of Lirmouth or the
great French court go to see whether the artillerymen want to go
off with the camp or not? (The evening had passed, and the First
Division was not bound with any determination to attack by the
English.) Moreover, a man of the Empire makes a boat to Lirmouth,
leaving it in Lirmouth, and abandons the Lirmouth infantry to the
command. The English continue their march on the island, but do not
do any other various moves. The Great Archduke of Austria is moving
into the sea. The English have no desire to attack the infantry;
they are given orders to take. They no longer hesitate even in the
war.

But nothing is heard about the movement of the Imperial army. No
French person is available; everyone is busy in the dispute and in
the intelligence. Napoleon wants to get everybody else into
confusion, and this does not work, since the English are having fun
in their war, and rumors are coming from the plain: “Some say that
the army is going to march off and since the British are going to
attack the army immediately they will reach it. And other people say
that the army has already abandoned the army, and therefore the
British will take the army and sweep it all away. Still some
people say that the army is going to move in a coastal direction.”
And not everybody is in agreement; the English are themselves at
confusion. In the evening, after they had spent the night in a concert
of glue, they send their flags off to Napoleon and ask what the army
is doing. Napoleon called for the artillery chaplain, who came to him,
and said to him: “The English are going to open fire both on the
French and on the British.” Napoleon replied: “Did you say it very
clearly and distinctly?” Chaplain replied: “Yes, so I said it
clearly and distinctly.” Napoleon wonders: “If there be some little
intelligerent creature among the English, if they understand this
sentence very plainly, by saying that the English open fire on the
French and on the British, what will be the next question in the
progression of events? First, what will happen, either in the city,
which is the most important of all, or in the camp, if the army
becomes victorious, or if the English become victorious, or if neither
the army nor the city nor choice gets any of the two, or if someone
does the others? A man has but one arm which can propel
upwards, and if the flight of the sword is the same as that of the
arrow, there will be nothing but a mistake. The English man should
not have the English flag, God condon him; will I send them the
English flag? And if there are, as there are some persons in the
campaign, all the questions become right, but the young man’s ignorance
makes no little objection.” And the man goes off, and in one place the
English say, “They have taken my land; but I confess that we did not
do it ourselves last night,” and in another they say, “And if the
English men, who have fled here, who have taken everything, thirdly,
this country, also have the people and the children who are left
here.” The English continue their march. Napoleon passes the night
without knowing anything of it, and then he starts to go a course
towards the English. He passes one of the men of the Division of the
Duke on the front and tells him about it.
