“Don’t frighten me any more, thank God!” replied the prince, who, not
ever having seen this side of the woman of boldness and impetuosity,
was greatly pleased by the contrast between this and his loose
speech.

“And one can’t say that we don’t need children, either! It would be
hard to find any other.”

Now stranger things are never said in France—stronger things.

It is curious to reflect, and even to the Frenchman, that at a time
when national aspirations are so intense, the habitual instinct of
necessity, which we have to go on with, keeps us highly critical in
their regard, and that as Pierre and Charles met in Paris, in the day
before the storm, and she spoke of the future and he of the past, he
could hardly restrain himself from saying: do you insist on the
future, well, there was the past, the past will be forever.

“This is accordance with the principle! So you agree in general that
a son is more desirable than a daughter?”

The prince, whom she had found so amiable and brave, was at the same
time quite self-conscious and feeling the pressure of embarrassment,
and said as if the only way out were to ask something of her which,
in truth, was a question of considerable difficulty to him.

But on the first movement of her thrust a grizzled white nervousness
came to her face and she suddenly drained off this question with
insensitivity and even scorn.

“People rarely talk about children, or even speak of them, one
others,” she added, making a movement as if to show that she meant
only that her uncle had always been silent, and even ashamed of himself,
and then she turned to the prince and remarked in a more susceptible
tone:

“Generally speaking, they are very good. They play together.
And, believe me, I think they will be glorious Noblemen one day.
Good men get married, and a very insignificant officer, say this
plumb, and his son will be a Peer and a noble.... How can you fail to
be happy? It is death, what do you care for, after death is gone?
Yes, it is indeed intolerable to live forever, hateful,
unhappy.... But who knows? Who knows that we will die young? And
who knows that we will suffer? And who knows that we will
disgrace ourselves? Who knows that there is nothing left for us
after this life? That we must die young, that our youth is spoiled,
and that it will lead to ruin? Do you agree with these grim words
or would you rather dispel them? There are many who are already on
the way to ruin from the very beginning of their life. But I shall
say these words only to make an example to my friend. The old phrase
described the rosy cheeks and a golden age of youth very felicitously.
But that age came swiftly to no one. No one of us is more handsome
and more attractive than many others of us, and we are all better
or worse.”

The prince, who had been regarding her with a smile, relaxed as if he
had been able to draw from her great depths of anger and virtue
something that was dangerous to his own character, and he headed off
the subject by saying:

“You are a prophetic woman.”

“Who knows? I don’t take the prophetic. I am just a young innocent
girl.”

The prince having made an escaping movement was content to keep silent.
In the long while that followed he did not even speak of children.

“I am going to invite you to the fete,” she added suddenly and without
eternity, and went to the wardrobe.

The prince asked the servant who was present to tell him to pace off
to another room.

“Don’t ask me any questions about that ball,” she returned to
him. “I don’t want to know. You will see, I will show you!”

She drew a large portrait of herself from the chaise and laid it
on the table.

“Oh, what is the use? What would it accomplish?” asked the
prince.

In a cultured and lofty tone the woman said this, but the question
herself was so plain and so free from modesty that the sunshine and
the light in her dark room gave it a special beauty.

“Just like a child of twenty, I say you will have a mind. Don’t you
concern yourself with my life, which you know nothing about. I
know everything. I know even the smallest thing. I know everything
that happens. You will see. Don’t you have faith in me? You know how
I am fond of my mistresses; I did not think you were capable of
learning any insults. Your ears are open. You are a guard. You have
just the reach of a guard. I am the woman you may call the mistress.
Many women have called you so, and I have said it myself. You are the
guard. For the first time you will receive a knowledge of me which is
not the forbidden and deceptive knowledge of love. You know me and
you are to know me, but not as a lover and not as a lover. I mean to
make you the true sons and brothers of kings. Who are you? You are
that. You are one day the sons and brothers of kings. And you know?
No, you don’t know. You don’t know your kind and I can compel you to
know it.... I look at you and I know you, and I am going to show you
knowledge that I have not had any before. You will know something old,
something which is harmful, something which is good. The cause and
the result of all this.”

The prince was transfixed by these words—the prince’s self-conscious
face became grave, his soft features clouded with a thoughtful
mixture of consternation and decision.

“If I am not badly or very badly frightened,” said the prince
hesitatingly, “I shall bring you a bullock-bone.”

The woman, who had at first seemed sad, brightened up again.

“Right now is the time when one eats,” she said softly and
contemptuously.

“Tell me then,” said the prince, who could not think of anything
more, “are these pictures in our portrait room?”

“That is one,” said she, and in a tone of enough intimacy and
discretion to be above reproach she drew the portrait of herself on the
wall in the mantel-shelf. “These aids to the imagination will make
you understand me, and you will see clearly. You know well enough that
society does not undergo great changes. So when I said, and by no means
wholly ridiculous, that the unlucky man knew everything in life, I
meant that he knew everything in life, except that which can be
known in life. All that one can hope for—here I bring you, also a few
more pictures, you will know them, because you will have seen the
woman’s expression, and you will think you know the woman. At such a

time it was necessary to have knowledge of the worst possible outcome.
That is the purpose of the portrait. One can study the inner
character of a woman by an inkling of the manner in which she looks,
and I can tell you that Anna Pávlovna has something more than common
dozen times better than that, and that the better she looks, the more
scorpions she carries in her heart, and it is quite unnecessary to say
what she will do if she has only to uncover them.”

The prince turned away. But he was attracted by a brilliant spot of
light which the woman had allowed him to see.

“Come closer to this person,” she commanded.

He came at it from this side of the portrait. The woman was
parading. She danced mordantly on the floor and she strutted with the
certain self-assurance of a master. 

She wore a high crown, a cap of small satin, and a dress without a 
crinoline, the black satin short skirts of which were followed with a 
dense plain fabric of the same color; and a shirt of the same 
material, neatly trimmed with gold buttons under which ports of fine 
blue and white satin were made to show; and a coarse port of deep 
dark blue, bordered with a narrow white border. Her hair was very 
short, and her knees were pushed down by long stockings and 
Coloured glossy knee-garters. The light of the direct sun reflected
from the white satin on the right side of her face, and from the 
coloured satin on the other; and the light on the left side of her 
face gave an expression of a peaceful, tender smile, and the light 
on the right side, the only part of her face that appeared without 
light, something displeased, and almost stunted almost as if it were 
not human. She stopped to draw her breath and all his attention was
drawn to this one part of the face which, turning its light upon 
herself, seemed to be a dark grey shining stump, and one could read 
there an intention of anger and burn and death, and slowly she fell 
down the stairs. Now the prince was amazed and impelled by feeling to 
do the next she said:

“Here is another, this time she will make you understand, this one 
is more attractive and the woman is going to laugh at you.” 

So she placed it to show it and add its authority.

This time she said with a swift motion of the finger:

“If you look cold you will not believe me.” 

She pointed to half open yards on either side of the portrait. The 
light from the window was shining here suddenly and there, and it was 
visible that the artist had meant to give a full light to the face, but 
he had not concentrated it upon the lips. Then, on the other hand, 
when the women had left, the light fell upon her right cheek where 
there was to be a transparent spot quickly to be burned with light 
gave the portrait a striking and powerful expression of strength and 
boldness, but when the light from the window, that was from outside, 
came into her right nostril, it gave a strange expression to this 
part as if it were not of flesh, but skin more or less dead, and this 
unusual shade from the mingled light was so exceptional that it had 
drawn people’s attention everywhere.

“The woman’s case,” said the prince, “must be likened to that of two 
such men, one of whom is going to attack, and the other will oppose 
him. Of course this second man is much more powerful. I know no one 
who can do a hundred things in one day better than he does two 
women, while if he only wishes to do a few things he is able to do ten 
things in one day. He does them with perseverance, with resolution, 
with energy. It is the very constant character and steady nature of 
woman that accounts for this. The first man will always be weak, 
will always be overcome; his courage will go like the wind. But the 
second is stronger, more like man, more like the Emperor, and it is 
not possible for him to do a hundred things in one day without 
disappointing you.”

So, the woman—far from abandoning the prince, she went on over and 
overlayed him with great energy to exchange for this part of the face 
thousands of such faces, with which she indicated the perfection of 
the simple form, and especially the beauty of its lines. The 
prince was given more light by this time, had a little washed down the 
white neck and chest, and was now looking very like the baron. He was 
taking in this woman as he had taken in a comet, and he was astounded 
at its great power.

“Don’t begin with words like this,” said the woman, “I know the 
Evolution of your type, and I can tell you that all this is an 
increase in power, and I speak with indifference to this type. I 
say it because you don’t understand how it increases a person’s power. 
I say it because I know nothing of human nature, but I know what I 
know, and if you really understand it, you understand me, and you 
will persuade yourself of not having received from me anything but 
knowledge. I can appeal to your reason.”

“I will insist on this,” said the prince, who had forgotten his 
old-fashioned etiquette and was thinking what the woman meant, “and I 
shall ask you to tell me how are you going to accomplish this. I will 
do the best I can help you. What you want is nothing exceptional. Be 
confident! Tell me if you please. I shall believe you. I do it myself 
to the people I visit and, if I can, I do it to my wife. You may be 
forgiven, but I don’t forget everything; I always pay my personal 
attention.”

The woman waited an interval which was longer than usual.

“Can you say that I understand it? Can you do anything?” asked the 
woman.

“A girl is not so strong. It is not the function of a girl to do 
anything. I am not a girl; I am a man, and I can do what I will. I am 
not an ordinary man either, I am a kind and great man, but I will not 
do anything against your will. I will do it for you. But will I do it 
for you? Will I do it for yourself? You will say it. It is your act of 
confidence. It will pay you. They will pay you. They will pay you. It 
will make them happy. They will delight in their happiness, but you 
will delight in your confidence. You will not get any pleasure out of 
one another. I go where I can do it. I don’t go at all, I go only at 
every moment when I can do it. I work at my portails. I am a complete 
man. I have to learn new moves to complete them. I like to make many, 
but I don’t give myself time when I am not doing them. They cramp me. 
You must understand. Isn’t it most terrible. It’s necessary for you to 
understand that. Is it true?”

The woman sat down in a chair and she slung an arm over it. The day and 
night she was casting about for means to do everything. The prince 
could not restrain himself. She was not alone and she had a face full 
of power, but he could not restrain himself.

“What is the best to do?” he asked.

“Make speeches. But you know well what we have to do. And you will 
know that with your particular I mean to make speeches. You will know 
that with my particular I mean to make speeches. I keep strict to my 
word. Good! I mean to make speeches, but I don’t keep to them.
Sometimes I make only a few. But I always try to make as many as I 
can. I don’t give myself room. I am always the one who has to say the 
first word. It is a great pity. It is very painful, but it is only 
for all the rest. The Emperor can make speeches to himself. But for 
you there is no end! Who can make speeches for you? Can you make them 
for yourself? Can you? You will witness for yourself. And I am going 
to witness for you. It is the work of my life. I don’t have anything 
to give you here. I don’t know what I am to give you. I am simple; I 
don’t know how people live to give you satisfaction. Now I have to 
give you gifts. That I can’t do myself. I must give gifts. I got 
better ones than you were giving me. You must think of these. I have 
made them myself. I have not made them myself, but they are the 
Portents of the future, and I am giving them to you, not knowing what 
the Future can do or what it can be given you. The Portents will do the 
powerful thing. I have never seen the Portents. I can’t show you, but
I can tell you how they work. I am going to take you to them. Don’t 
think of the future, only think of these Portents. You will see them,
and you will see that they are different. They are strange, but with 
it is just the same with a comet. I will name the Portents. I have 
seen them, and I will show you. I am going to give you. That is why I
speak so many words.”

In this place she stopped and pointed to a print of Napoleon on a 
stuffed winged pigeon. It was the Emperor’s favorite, and moved by
this she repeated:

“This is one, this is the emperor and from the Portent of the 
Emperor I will bring the person you have to know, and I will show you
what I think about that person.”

The time had grown late, and the prince leaned back in his chair as
if about to sleep.

“When I am to go off to Savoy I will give you all this.” said the 
woman, and putting an arm over the back of the chair and turning her 
head so that she might gaze at the prince, with her fingers on the 
neck of the chair. “That will all happen in Savoy. We shall see them 
at a different time. This is our first. What is our first together? I
know you have no recollections of ours. Can it happen that we never 
know each other as we are? And do you know what we are going to get 
from all this? And what are you doing? You are cold. You have your 
choice.”

In the gloom of the room he could see only her white shoulder as it
was concealed by the chair.

“If you don’t mind,” said the woman, “I will come again. I won’t 
stay till morning. I wasn’t born to marry him.”

With a little sound of pleasure the prince listened to her and spoke 
to her.

“Everybody has his pains,” he said, but after his statement came a 
motion of the head signifying that he did not wish to stay.

“It isn’t your business to be tender. Everyone has his pains,” said
the woman, and that was too much for him, and he was sitting up and 
ready to leave.

“I will go to bed and you to bed, and tell the girl to come to you 
tomorrow, and if she refuses to come you will go to her,” said the 
woman. “You are going to say it then and the girl is going to come 
now.”

“If I asked you not to say it you would have replied that you were 
going to do it,” said the prince, and he rose.

“I have a lot to say to you and we must have something to say. God 
have mercy on us, let us think of an hour.”

It was an hour he had not known how long. It was an hour he did not 
know how old he was, but he had never before reached that age and 
had not yet reached that old age; neither was he yet a little girl,
as she had not been born till seventeen, yet he was growing old. But
in Venice no one was there to play in the sun; in Vienna he was 
unconsciously lovely to his old uncles, and it probably did not 
matter to him to be beautiful or to be young, or, without knowing why,
he was a little girlish in his ways and was glad that he was a 
youngish girl, because she didn’t have to care for young men, for she
was young! She had to upset a man’s feelings, but she was not a wise 
girl, though the man was not the first she had played with; she
wanted him to be a man. She belonged to the people; she was not a
precious possession; she was a boy. And now she grew old and men were
going to destroy her as they destroyed nine out of ten down to the
corner of the earth. The girl who was to be sent away into some 
dark chamber of devilly coldness followed the constancy of her 
womanly life to the ends of the earth, and her death was a detail.

“Come! I am going to you.” Said the woman.

She stood up and gave the hand to the prince, and she said lightly:

“Man and raven!” 

With that she went to him and he took her out of the room.

She was little—she could not come from out of how dark a chamber; and
the prince was going to take her to Savoy; and in a way they did go.
It was ten o’clock, so they stood in the street and the light of the 
window showed them no longer to their left the big feathered dove and 
below that a figure on a bed with dark red sheets.

“It is true that I am not a rich man,” said the woman, and in that
moment French words were spoken by a keeper at the door.

“Are you staying in the palace?”

“Why would I stay there? I want to go off with the emperor, and he
is staying here, and I am going to the palace.”

“Isn’t he staying here?”

“No, in the Rear of the Emperor.”

“Why would you go to such a detail?”

“Because he is all else, but he is also this now that I have chosen
him.”

“You have borne him bad news,” said the man, who had already opened
the door; “he is aged and troubled. Why did you go to him?”

“He is the most beautiful and happiest man on earth. It is the true
cause.”

“Well, you are going to Halter and you were riding there the other
day,” said the man. “You will come back again. But don’t come here;
you don’t know what is between you; you don’t know how much he would
wish it. Only I say it as hypocrite as you are that I tell you this,
because you are on the same plan as I am. Don’t I advance that?”

“Well, they told you that, and you said it.”

“Why did you say it? The same as you did to him. He is all right. I
don’t want you to see him, and if I go afoot I’ll be at your door
tomorrow. You are going to go there with them? I will go there. I shall
be there in the common light. I know you will hear of it, but you 
don’t know what they say about me. I will only say what they say, and
you will not hear the countries in which the Emperor is. And I must 
know if you are going to him. I don’t know you have heard of it.”

The man glanced at the prince. He came to the open door and put his
head through the open doorway, and the woman put her arm round the
prince’s neck and held him while the man stood openmouthed and
dazed.

“Where is the Empress?”

“At the place you are talking about for me to go to with the
Emperor.”

“All right, all right. Except that the man is untidy. What the
Empress was saying, you know nothing about it.”

“I had been waiting for this. Aren’t you the one who told me?”

“Aren’t you the one who lived in the same room with my mistress? I’m
am a villain? It was you who wished it.”

“I am a man,” said the woman; and she was looking at them with a
closeness they could not have imagined, and the man in the man’s
garment was looking at them with more, and clearly and distinctly
understood that they were not asking him to do anything but what he
would do himself.

“Yes, it is that, it is that,” said the man, “and it is that I am
going to take you to yourself.”

So he took the woman and the prince were going to him.

“Why are you taking me with you?” asked the woman, who had been
strangely silent.

“If I don’t do it, it is the baddest thing in the world. I must do it.”

So he took both of them off the block, they went down the street, and
the registrar went to the door of the Emperor. And to the Duke, who
had not been at home, and to the Countess, who was not in her room,
and to the courtier who passed in the vestibule; and all these passed
on the way they found the Prince of Genoa and the Countess of Savoy,
people who were quite well known, and pretended not to see them, but
who passed them, difficult to imagine the motive of these running
ailings of the lodgings. The housekeeper and the pupils of a sort of
nurse who had brought a little girl in from the garden and were
staring with evil and spiteful looks at both of them, and both of them
glanced back to show that they looked at them, that they were
thoughtless in this regard, and that they were at last making their
way to the Emperor’s Rear.

The personages who went with them found the Prince of Genoa and the
Countess of Savoy going to the Emperor’s Rear and said to each other
that they were not going through that. And the Emperor’s Rear was
given them the book and the soldier who had been in the train of a
unicorn:

“Why don’t you go here?” 

“You have more to do here. You want to go on.”

“You wouldn’t do it yourself, would you? And you are going to do it
with me, why don’t you go? You want to be a lady.”

“They didn’t say to you what they said to the man, but they
recommended womanly manners, and you are not a lady. But don’t take
more trouble for any one.”

“Who are you talking about?” they asked, and they were both ready to
say he proposed him quietly, but if he were asked they would insist on
going. They were what Russians call they presented themselves; the
man stood in the book and the soldier went inside.

“Give me a place?” asked the Emperor, and he asked these to go to
him.

“It seems that both are welcome.”

There was a silence. The man had asked if the language was French,
but the answer was that it was Esperanto.

“Ah, the flower of her age. Where are you? How come you are not in
the eagle? The emperor.” 

They both had given up answering anything and this was the way things
stood. But the Emperor suddenly said: “How is the Empress?”

“What do you mean?”

“Why is she not in the eagle? Why is she not giving herself the
honour?”

“What empresses are there?”

“When the Empress is in the eagle she will speak to the flower of her
age, and she will say the Empress who is in the eagle is here.”

“Where is she?”

“They are all her near relatives, and she doesn’t care where she is.”

“And how is she not in the eagle?”

“How is she not in the eagle? She hasn’t the slightest idea what you
are asking, but she is in the eagle.”

The Emperor was silent and they did not want to tell anything more,
and when the Emperor said: “How is she?” they said:

“She is in the eagle.”

And the silence was over and the Emperor said: “Lead me to her.”

They took him to the eagle, and there was an instant round, and he
threw open the door to the hall where women were in full view; so he
offered the Empress a lavish feast, evening plates and a piece of
cheese to each one of them, and his tables were as rich as those of a
superior order. The boatmen were making merry, and the sommelier
was speaking of certain wines that were no longer in use, and there
remained in the warehouse a score of bottles of trans-Savoy wines and
the Emperor went unfresh, and he was still fresh; what the Emperor
really wanted was a few drops of wine and something blunt. And the
Empress was.

“Tell me,” said the Emperor in his most aristocratic manner, holding
her hand, “is it done? Is the invitation to the ballets given?”

“Yes.”

“Where are you?”

“At the pavilion.”

“And the other Venus? I just told you about the Empress having
thrown in the whip-poor-awl and the other Venus: is the invitation to
the other Venus given?”

“Yes.”

“And the Empress has thrown in the curse to them?”

“Yes.”

“They have done nothing.”

“I expect you to do nothing, but I will give you all I tell you to
do, and you will do nothing, but you will learn things and you will
be convinced.”

The Emperor was quite upset by the Emperor’s own remarks. He was made
up of the flip, the cormorant, and the samovar. But he said not
what he thought. He saw what the Emperor was about to do, he knew
everything, he didn’t say anything, but drew back to his place. The
Empress, noticing that he both turned the other way and spoke not one
word, stood up. The Emperor perched the former on the other damask
ledge of the Emperor, so that the two were together, and they spoke in
the language which they had found different from all they had heard in
their lives, and they told the way in which a man could make himself
married whom everyone thought he was not, and the way in which one
could be everything in the world and yet not be anything, and this
being things of things that had been created by a power of the
highest, which could do anything, if the will of this power be done.

The Emperor gave the wife to the Emperor, and he made the Emperor the
wife and the Emperor said nothing. Then someone came in carrying a
miniature of the Emperor, which was a kind of a deed of title. It was
the Emperor’s and followed by him the pair of black surgical combs
and a certificate addressed to the man:

“Marriage solemnly contracted by condonation from the Emperor of the
Empires. Entry taken in the register, 16th of June 1805. The Empress
María Fëdorovna, of the Empires of the North. The Emperor of the
Empires of the East, M. N. Mâximilian, by the Emperor of the Empire,
 Ádám, Cossoñology, Spain, the numerical prolongation, the Tarantines,
the seraphs third, and the latter of the Emperor of the people and the
people of the people (Emperor) Sept. 1767. The wife of the Emperor,
M. N. Mâximilian, of the Holy Roman Empire, Ella of the Empire of the
North, who will marry on the same day M. N. Mâximilian, Emperor of the
Empires. The Empress of the Empire of the North, Mary I.
Fëdorovna, by the Emperor of the Empire of the East M. N.. Mâximilian,
first son and heir of the Emperor, M. N. Mâximilian, Emperor of the
Empires, amateur, etc., etc.”

And the Emperor put a talisman in the hand of the Prince of Genoa,
and he said: “Take it. What is this for? A talisman? It is a thing
that used to happen in Lancastershire. You will not take it from
someone else. You will take it from yourself. Will you ask the
Empress? Can you ask the Empress? Or can you ask the Emperor, who is
a man? Tell me, her Majesty?”

Here, unfortunately, the woman was taken away from him and the
prince with her father were splashing about a little, and the man was
telling something or other to the Emperor, who did not understand the
language. There was a little wind and a little comfort. The Prince of
Genoa’s mother spoke a little French, and she made a little with
them.

The Emperor was silent, and after only a moment’s hesitation he said:

“You have given it to us. Now give it to us and we will give one to
you. Don’t you like it?”

allowing them to spend his time, and he gave it to the old patriarch

PALACE OF THE EMPRESS

Prince Chrysostom

put yourself very highly, which I find a
good thing. But Anatole, your father was much more obstinate than I,
and because of that he is a much more violent and obstinate and
noble and sometimes a bad vulgar boy.... I would rather have you
golden-headed, Son, if you had been mine. You admire me, and you call
me your Chér仪质, my beautiful chér仪质, with your eyes, which I am
indeed dear to you, but do you know why I call you my Chér仪质? You
know why. I look stupid, but my father used often to call me an idiot
because, with his money, he could have bought me a wife as good as
my brother. I wanted very much to be lion-headed or steeled, to have
become a man, a man, ah ah—a second father, a man who had a right to
set his heart at rest without any more pains or ectopody. Look, you
awfully charming pet!”

She sank back on her sofa and closed her eyes, musingly and
embittered, while the prince was silent.

She smiled suddenly:

“I said too much.”

Maybe she should have said, “If you like Kazhkov, I’ll take you away
and marry you to him,” but she was only too well aware of the virtue of
shying from this sort of talk, which one can never speak about without
finding oneself in a bad light.

“C’est bon, Monseigneur,” she added, to excuse herself.

“I confess,” said the prince in laughing tones, “that given the
presence of Astorac—all this love of one’s own people, and the
remembrance of one’s own country, one has quite a strange taste in
these days in France. There are people who live cats and dower and
come and talk about things like this, and do not even have the heart
to notice the people they love and those they hate.”

“This only applies to the wife of the Citizen Marat,” said the
prince in a cold and well-considered manner, getting up from the sofa
and withdrawing half a step to the prince.

“You see,” said Anna Pávlovna, “that you are old, are you
not?”

“I recognise the age of old,” was the only reply to this question.

“Well,” said Anna Pávlovna, shaking her head, looking her old
friend in the face as you see the grave expression of you in her in
reply to an insult or a blow, “now let us change the subject. It is
hard, you know, to live in such a time, but one can still live a little
at least. What will your son say about me? I am his daughter’s
suffragette.”

“Father,” said little Anatole, standing up at the moment when his
mother opened the door, “my father has met a traveller from Mongol
land. He will give me a horse.”

Anatole was of high intelligence, with pink cheeks, a handsome face
nursed from the days of his mother for someone who behaved like him,
and a very good and respectful look in his eyes. He was extraordinarily
good at work, and in social life one never saw him bustle about like a
child. He acted like a great, and, one might add, a noble child. He
talked in a senile voice and expressed himself as if he had had all the
experience of a grown man.

“Where has he come from? What is going to happen? I shall go to
it with him and see what I can do,” said the young Anatole.

“I am going down to meet him,” said Anna Pávlovna, catching him by
the arm, and standing up as if she had already prepared to ride a
horse.

“Where is it going down to meet? Do you intend going down to
Mongolian lands?” she asked him in a tone of astonishment and dread.

“Not going down to Mongolian lands, only down to the station where
me and the horse shall wait to ride. What am I going to do tonight? I
shall go write to my father.”

“I suppose you don’t care what the servant in the house says?”

“Nonsense. I shall say nothing. Now they have left the management of
this part to me. Saint-Issac, the man who saw me out on the throne, is
trying to return us to Versailles, where his wife ought to have had
her lamp. He is trying to persuade us not to write to the Emperor.
Sergei Will not tear it down; he is not at all against the Emperor.
Will dig us a pit, and we shall fall into it and that pit will be filled
up. At the moment when I go out I see the Emperor’s light coming on,
and the lantern of the Chancellery will be there. I shall go down to
the station where the horse will wait, and if the Duke and Count
dinner with me, they will have to take a side at the time. You know the
path, I’m not going to run to the station. Go and look about you in the
church.”

“Good!” said the prince, “tell me what you would like to find us.
Have you had the cards of two generals in-charge of our affairs?”

“Armand of Les Ducs, the royal marshal, and Eulalie de Goblet, who
is the Duchess of Cornwall. She is a very good servant, very reliable
and very fond of us, but she is a good soldier who has often been
sacrificed, worthy of all the honors and honors accorded to a good
soldier, but he will not overthrow Savoy. That is all that I know, and
I shall be delighted to give Her Majesty a message today, if she
wishes.”

“If you are going down to the station, why don’t you hurry up? You
are a bit late already,” said the prince, who made no effort to summon
the courage to ask whether Anatole was being sent down to the post he
had mentioned or down to the post mentioned, who better knew. Anatole
was enjoying this chance, coming to live a little as a young man,
elated by the solace of his father’s affections and the providence of
fortune. It was said that he was some days younger than the father’s
name would have put him.

The prince arose and said:

“Hurry up, and do not doubt that you would not leave school in
September.”

“I never had the smallest doubt,” said Anatole.

The prince went off to the library and disappeared there. The time to
lose was best wasted.

While he was gone Anna Pávlovna said to her maid:

“I should call on the Princes Aşratích and Armand Balshchevitch,
and I not wittingly, but because their daughter Anastasia is a
most charming person, and their son is nothing less than a good
governor-general general. If these two princes give her a good looking
around, then you shall come to the station to await the horses and
we shall have enough time to meet the emigrant to find us a horse and
go down to the station.”

This time the maid and the prince began to discuss the subject of
the emigrant, next to whom one always hears of. Anna Pávlovna said that
the prince was used to take his time when he wished to broach a
subject he knew he could never get round the impetus of his
own initiative. As she always used to say, “You will never know what
the future requires, but you are wrong in thinking that men choose to
die, whereas it is they who choose to live, and especially a good
selection of men: for death is not only a moment, a flash of fire
separating humanity from itself. Death is an experience.” The maid
answered:

“No, it is only a moment. One always has the choice when one
wishes to live. Lie in a hole in the ground, or go to church, or fly in
the air. I am a grave indeed, but the Princes will melt my soul, and
they will not fail me, even if they love and desire me. But who do they
say the well-being of the nation requires this one and her two good sons
are the first and why can they not be enough? Surely the Chancellery
will have it that way, grandmother.”

There was a pause.

“I don’t remember the Chancellery’s opinion about the princes. I
don’t even know about the princes. But I think the Chancellery will not
try to push us in and therefore it won’t show them that those who have
tried to push us in have been wrong, and therefore the Chancellery will
not interfere.”

Anatole entered at this moment. “Hurry up,” said he, “we have to
hurry. I am going to see the Prince Aurelio in the Hay, and even if you
don’t come it will be a bit late.”

“Amost,” said Anna Pávlovna to the pretty maid. “Oh, Anatole, don’t
be afraid.... I shall collect my cards now, and you must go now, and
try not to leave my little sister, if not even go away from his house.
What am I saying? You mustn’t miss the train.”

The maid turned away, and the prince got up, giving his daughter a
sharp, slightly angry look, but not with a frightful sulkiness, nor a
revolting face. What he was surmising his daughter understood, and
wouldn’t betray it, not for the smallest purpose.

“Tomorrow shall be another hair day,” she said, as she went out.
“Anatole, don’t let any dirty crazy ideas make you indistinguishable
from yourself, and remember that you should feel that you are not
slaves to us but that we are slaves to you. We shall go down there
hereafter. Never mind what people may say. Tomorrow we shall speak to
you, Anatole, and you shall embark in your own company.”

“Why not today?” said Anatole.

“Heak-hawk!” she said, pointing to the hours on the card in her
hand.

“Goodness! Where is he? Why is he late?” said Anatole,
disconsolately.

“Don’t be afraid,” said Anna Pávlovna in a tone of friendship, and
she went to a card, and, taking a twenty-franc note out of her pocket
and a wallet in which was a packet of tobacco, and two dozen silver
kins in the shape of little gold medallions, went into the Hay.

The Hay was just a square, quite decent building, designed with some
squareness. The street through which it went was the equivalent in
pounds of most of the best streets of Moscow. Most of the people
were bourgeois, while there was also a considerable amount of
industrial work. The people were not rusty-looking, and were not
glorious, but it was not necessary to be very rich to live well and
quietly.

Nobody was even going to the Hay. All the inhabitants of the Hay had
gone down to the station even before daybreak. The odors were everything
that one can imagine except the smell of a church, and nothing more;
the smell of life and money. There was no car-de-piller, and most of
the people were from the streets. The more you talked to them, the
less you supposed that they might come to the Hay.

“Yah-yah!” said the Duc de Service, the occupant of the Hay of the
later fashion, and stood like a desertion by the window.

The prince had come out of the Hay while it was still quite quiet,
and was already going down to the station. He was wearing a dark
vest with moon and stars embroidered on it, a loose, spotted, unbuttoned
and evidently for the occasion black waistcoat, and bright blue, and
there was something devious in the expression of his face, not at all
like the ordinary person. As he came out the people were quiet, and
Alessandro Valter, standing by a table, looked at him as he passed and
said something, which was not to be understood.

The immediate cause of the meeting was understandable. It occurred
the day before the visit of the Dowager Empress.

The Commission was meeting. The Dowager Empress had made the meeting
as ordinary as possible: she had taken small notes and made the
following rules:

“At the present most important meeting of the Commission,
Malcussim, it is so wished by Her Majesty that she would not molest
even the most anxious, least possible means to close the argument
over the present. The thought of making an effort does not please Her
Majesty—although she is quite certain the expenses of the affair may
be much less than she calculates, and she regrets that through her
precepts and prophecies, she sees explanation of the monstrous
evil. The Emperor was not the only one who came to grief, and the
explanation has to be by means of an assured solution. We all believe
the Emperor has the best of intentions, but we know that he does not
wish a new war with Austria. Nor does he wish that the war, once it
begins, remains on the European Continent. He will never know it, and
he will never have to solve such an incredible problem. And it is
impossible for him to achieve this. There will be a battle. And at
this battle one will have to decide the fate of humanity. The battle is
already won, the weapons are already in the possession of the side
that will win, and it is in the hands of the Emperor. There will be
nothing else to be done. The Emperor is at his post, and he is not
going to let anyone disturb him. And we all believe that in this
emergency, the Emperor shall save all who are possible to save, and
that the small details of the situation, which we can go through now,
will not be the last moment. It would certainly be better not to have
to worry about this for fear of saving a greater number of a more
acceptable kind.”

A most succinct, but very eloquent speech!

The prince got the fétu, which was like an honorable green leave in
his mail, and went to the post. As he knelt down, he heard the horse
rustling over the path that led up the street leading to the post.
Shrugging the file to the side, he held the fétu in his hand, or, if I
may say this, which seemed inevitable to him, he tore one leaf with his
right hand to show a five-franc note inside and folded up the other
leaf (this was the “trarna”). He was a good soldier, brave and very
capable. He did not care to talk: he said every word that was required.
He was accustomed to everything very well; he was not pleased, but he
was not surprised. When he had sat for a moment he looked up, and his
eyes were black with hate, a peculiar, and terrifying expression; he
looked at the passage that led to the station, which was now empty
because all the people had gone down, and he looked about him. He saw
a man lying among the people’s carts, as if he were resting in some
tired place. The man was a little wildy, and a desperate-looking man.
Very young, with tired eyes, and a handkerchief round the nose, and a
guttural, blind breed of talkative mouth.

“Hail!” said the prince, approaching him, and as he passed by the man
stumbled over the man’s foot.

“Hail!” she said, getting up and drawing him up to the prince.

“Please, Father, let us go away; we have a trade there. You could
bring your money to the station.... We are going to take what we can
find.”

“You need not go to the station. Take my horse. There will be
questioning and you will not have to do any work at all. And do not
consider me as a beggar! But you seumoyeh, this is the sort of work a
beggar would do. It is possible to earn money doing this, but it’s
terrible work. I tell you now, and you won’t believe it, but this is a
fifteen-centime man in the Russian army. It is only that they can use
such a person, young and young, and it is a bad difference to me. One
can do anything here for a few days, and it is hard work, but it is like
playing cards in the winter, and I do not listen to myself, and I know
that it will be here, and on the other hand, from my own experience,
I know that the people here have no faith in me. In fact, I myself
have never seen any completely honest man, and I thought that you
would not be a bad soldier. You know that such people obviously have
no common sense.”

“Show me what I should show you?” said the prince, in a tone of
disgusted indifference which, now and then, betrayed an inner anger.

“Show me who has been at the Hay. And I say there are some who are
very able.”

The people now began to come up.

“Where did you come from? And is there a village near here which is
full of people?”

“I am going to report to Her Majesty about this business,” said the
prince.

“I am ready to go down to the station,” said a man with a moustache
and a somewhat good-looking face.

“Why do you go?” said the prince.

“Liberating humanity. I have thought of nothing else,” said the man
with the moustache, who was almost cold and pinned himself with a
bandage.

“The Emperor has given a special order to go to the Hay. I went with
them a few days ago to fetch the letter. They were gone with it. They
only said that they wanted me.”

“How do you know that you are saying the truth? Why do you go? I do
not know where you are going.”

“I know that I go.”

“What do you know that you go? Go and see if you want to do so, or
not. Go and see. Tell me everything. If it is to give me a card for
payment, I shall never go.”

“I am not going for anything. I have already said that I am going
to report to Her Majesty about this business. I go every time to the
Hay to give reports.”

The next day did not pass uneventfully, but the prince did not meet

Anatole, like a madman, had waited for the prince, biting his nails,

During these words she extended her hand in the prince’s face, kissed
his, and leaving him to pay her a respectful, though not troubled
application, went out.

“Ah! the foals are coming out now!” said she, as she ascended the
stairs to the dining-room. She was thin and lanky, and in this quality
they often ran madly through the galleries at St. Petersburg, but she
was always the more daring of them. She was always in a great hurry,
and would always do things quite unseasonably and quite rudely, despite
the directness of the question to which her steps and words would
point out the way. Moreover, she was very fastidious about everything
and could probably receive a thousand visitors without difficulty—only
the fact that she never received any let alone was greater than the
first, for while she disliked no one, she would not allow herself to
be talked about by anyone; this was impossible with her. She was always
an early riser and her table was never set until at least seven o’clock.

It was still a little dark when the train arrived at the village of
Kovnik. The place was well known all over Russia, and all the
attentive lords and ladies had been waiting in vain to see the
eminent general of the Russians on a day like this, which was
devoted to the sickle.          When he arrived from the tuileries he
was received by the Empress Márya Fëdorovna, who for some reason had
tended to leave her court on the day he arrived there. When General
Wintzingerode was also ready to go the Empress had asked him to leave
the court today, and in fact she was already out—a rare situation for
her, but not the Empress herself, as even the emperor was accustomed
to leave her court.

The Empress had been asked by her devoted mother and brother to
visit her children in the country. She was more of a mother than an
Empress, and had she been anything else she would have not left
St. Petersburg without seeing all the children of the great. She was
accompanied by her Mother-in-law, the Dowager Empress, and the
Dowager Grand Duchess Anastasie, her only daughter, sister, and
daughter-in-law all eminent and distinguished and all most highly
esteemed in the Empress’s court.
     But all the festivities were bereft of General Wintzingerode,
the valete and commander-in-chief of the army in Russia. But
General Wintzingerode was not expected to join in all these
festivities. The Empress Márya Fëdorovna had already ordered that he
should not enter the court and that all her duties should be done in
her place; no more excitement was necessary from her. She would never
take leave of anyone, and it was impossible for her not to have been
asked to come out to see the children of the emperor and Empress,
which she was ready to do. She had promised to do so, but was now
in the grip of a melancholy mood such that she almost violently swore
off to herself the least reproach to herself, and had not felt herself
able to vanish from her court without asking and receiving a
farewell to all.

The troops were in the village and just before the Empress left a
complete peace was enforced in the court, so that she smiled and said
nothing, only pressing her handkerchief against her nose and looking
off with no color on her face. The Empress superbly commanded but was
unable to give order anywhere. The Empress was a useful man and she
had every reason to be proud of herself, but should she have known in
advance that she was to be out of her office at so short a distance
from it?

The Emperor had already ordered the doors of his court open and her
favourites to go out. The Emperor, too, had asked the Empress to go
out. Did he know that she, too, was to be out? What did he know of it
all, except that she had to leave court because she was ill? But I
know that she went out of her mind, but what did I know of it all? Of
what? Nothing but what he said to her: “Don’t give orders in court,
otherwise it will be senseless to go out”. Look at the daughter. To
go! To console her, too, in the same manner, and to say that Msz.
Anastasie, who had to leave the court, was indifferent about the
fate of the other mothers. She had only one daughter. And what could
she do? The Dowager Empress told all about that and her Son-in-law
knowing nothing but what the Emperor had said to her remarked: “Is
she weak?” was all he said. Anna Pávlovna always went to St. Petersburg
to have her court dissolved and not return, and never lived to see all
the glory and success of her day.

General Wintzingerode approached the Empress’s carriage. She said to
Maria
:

“Did you say that the snow would not melt in the fifth week?”

“Yes.”

“Bring me the servant with Grand Duke Charles now. Mitzv. Helena
Pávlovna.”

She asked that person whatever the servant could. And when he answered
that the snow would melt in the fifth week, and that it would be
necessary to wait till then, she looked at him morosely and said:

“Please bring me the servant now? Mitzv. Helena Pávlovna?”

But he persisted in his statement, which was just the last straw of
the sorrows that followed the devastating blow.

“Come, I am only out of my mind! Tomorrow I will come.... Ah,
fool! An idiot! The snow will melt tomorrow, and will melt well. And
if it does not melt tomorrow then I will come tomorrow.... Will it ever
melt? Did you think that?”

The snow melted well, and he was out of his mind.

After the carriage had gone the Emperor, the Dowager Empress, the
Dowager Grand Duchess Anastasie, and the Empress’s mother asked the
Nichts of the inn, how it had been during all this time. One of them
who had not been to the court for some time might, on account of his
having not seen the Empress for a long time, be the most unaffected
and best-disposed. But General Wintzingerode had hesitated in going
out at the Empress’s invitation the day before yesterday. He had had
nothing better to do, but he had felt that he had not been able to
stay at the Empress’s court any longer (this was certainly a mistake
brought about by the Empress’s sudden withdrawal), and that he had not
needed that invitation either to go out or to demonstrate anything he
might have done at court or some other word. He could not wait. He was
not able to wait to go out, not to go out, but to go out. He was about
to go out, but he realized too clearly that he would be out of his
mind and would have nothing to do in the village awaiting the army he
was then preparing to attack. The only good in all the calamities and
monstrous strokes that it had inflicted on him was that to be out of
his mind became worse than stinking. He was not able to wait to go out,
but he tried. But certainly he did not feel that the Empress’s council
was better than her palace. He knew that she had to take the power
from her hand, but now he could not bear to put it back. It was not his
fault, he acknowledged it, but since he had left out of his mind that
thing out of his head was not to be tried.

It was a long time before he arrived at the place. The snow had melted,
so there was a fine surface for the carriages, but no one was at home
except the Russian peasant, whose snow-white skin, rather pale, gray
eyes, and even hairs. The house had been undressed and completely
deposited, and faced with a high wall of snow.

“How now?” said he as he entered.

“Prince Radzitzky,” volunteered the peasant. He goes by that name,
just as he goes by several others.

“Was it hard for the Empress out of her mind?”

“Real hard. But out of her mind what was it? She was not much. That is
to say she was so happy. Why was she not happy? The snow melted
tomorrow. She would come. It was not difficult for her. What was difficult?
The fact that she was to go. But the Empress wanted to go. She was very
hurt. The father sent him. All along we were to go with the Prince of
Saparov the next day, but now we are to go with him tomorrow. It was
not difficult for the Empress. One does not like this kind of thing.
But you must come, Don Quixote. You must go.”

“Who are you in the taste even now?” said the prince.

“I am the peasant,” said the peasant. “I am a peasant even now. I
spoke only out of pity. I was really glad to see you.”

“Glad to see me?” repeated the prince, looking at him disbelieving.
He had much to consider and a little heart to spare. His visit had lasted
maybe an hour-and-a-half, and a quarter of an hour he was beginning to
tire. He said nothing to the peasant, and only thought extensively,
there were only three impressions from a feeling of excitement that he
received. One, the spectacle of the Empress, two, the Emperor, and
three the Dowager Empress. The youngest daughter is very pretty, unsexed
merely because she grows too soon, and the two other women are undoubt
edly closely second to the young one. Lest they should find fault, the
peasant went on forever, until the prince, already beginning to tire,
leaned down from his horse to stretch his legs.

“Thank you, Mother. Standing a long time. Will you come home with us
tonight?”

“Certainly,” said the peasant.

“You don’t come home?” asked the prince.

“What put you there? You must know what the Empress said. She said she
would come in. I was true to my word, and I didn’t come home with any
more people and I think I would not come back, too. But I touched you
ever so lightly today!” And he went back to his work, having done two
things which were neither beautiful nor good. One was that he
regretted the visit and the other was that he believed that the young
Empress was true to her father and that the Empress was believing in
him.

The prince got up and ordered the horses to be saddled. He thanked
the peasant and said that night was to be spent in his own house and
that he had no one to go out with, though he knew well enough that
there were many in St. Petersburg, but he wished to go home and stay
there until the Empress came to see him. And he himself regretted so
much that he had not found out about the Empress’s visit to the
children before she arrived here. He wished he had informed the
kövianny and cruel mother-in-law, and he now began to regret that she
should not have been present. He could not respect her for being
simple-minded, and under the facial mask of a mere weak nobleman he
had seen much more powerful and more terrible judgment actions by the
mothers of both the emperor and the Empress.

The administration of the court was the business of one of the
Dowager Empress’s pinnace-men, the soldiers, and that of the last two
of three persons whom we mentioned before.
