And the prince, blood running cold through his veins, replied:

“Not at all. And in fact I don’t love them; I don’t know what
happened to them and I don’t have any family.”

Anna Pávlovna had become serious again.

“The happiness of all is connected with the happiness of the
adults,” said the prince vehemently, putting down his teacup.

“I don’t believe deeply in this theory either,” she replied in an
emphatic voice.

“Bless me,” said the prince, somewhat affronted, “don’t take my
sermons to heart. The happiness of the adults is just the price of the
love of gods.”

“And now we are to be going to town. You will have to do your
duty.”

The prince arose, shaking her hand, and said:

“I don’t know what to say to you.”

“Don’t say that. As you say, this is a yellow Jacobin, and he only
wants a bird to fly away from him as quickly as possible.”

The prince went to the door; and Anna Pávlovna, as she was about to
step out, called out, almost in a whisper, in tones of passionate
sadness:

“Inverkie, it is fun to die! What is the difference between my
death and that of one who, more bitter and cruel than I, dies at the
will of the dogmas of a whore?”

The prince started, rushed to her, and threw himself upon her knees,
and better still, in an ecstasy of faith and deferred impotence,
taking her in his arms:

“Don’t speak like that! My dear friend! At least don’t say it in my
presence.... This is my last speech.... Yes, I could not...”

He glanced at Anna Pávlovna with tears down his cheek, and added:

“in a moment so long that I shall meet Emilio and Marta.”

“God save them, Prince!” she cried, before she dropped to the ground.

As she lay down, however, she remained in her restlessness; that she
would not go to bed, gave her soul the impression of a man who had the
integrity of a hero, who had not been overcome by despair, and who
would rather die than live unjustly. But this thought had escaped him
only when, at that moment, in her feelings for this royal
tender-necked maiden, who was going to “be a cock’s-nipple of a
killing!” she suddenly gave way, for it was true that Anna Pávlovna
was mad, and for she was indeed mad. But she had been pretending to it
since she was twelve years old; and now her insanity, seeing the
moment when the burden of her present life became too heavy for her,
was like a new burden.

Thus, on the evening of 1st August, she did not go to bed.

It was a delightful evening. And thus in July, at the beginning of the
VIIIth Year of the French Empire, 22nd July, it happened that a
baronet, in his forties, of a most distinguished and agitated
character, and who spent all his time at court, was entertaining Anna
Pávlovna Schérer.

_Paul V,_ in a letter which he had written several years before, had
complained of the “civic and educational life of the metropolis,” and
had compared it to an “unequal, terrible, and singular city of the twelfth
century.” He had said there were only two great manufactures in the
length of ten leagues (Moscow and St. Petersburg); one was commerce
and the other manufacturing.

The Baronet, well to do like his mother, could afford a sum of five
hundred rubles a month, which declared to be a sum well earned by
labor. But his wife was a person of no higher intelligence than herself,
and he very soon perceived that it was a very difficult work to
further her education by paying her for pinches of bread and the use
of not a small proportion of a surplus income. He was indispensible
and dependent, and she was a strong person with a big head; she was
fervent and strong, but her habits were unpromising.

“I live,” said her eldest daughter—“like a woman. I live in the
market-place, where I bought it from the merchant. I go to chapel, and
in Passover I go with my husband to the funeral of the Bishop of
Leningrad, where is stops high crucifixes and where I could get a
suitable place. I say that industriously, and I do not mean only to
repeate my words.”

The Baronet’s wife, a woman of “something of a veneer,” but most
probably the finest creature in St. Petersburg, was only enthusiastic
in her home. She was devoted, warm and laudable, and carried on a regular
way of saying good-bye to other people’s children about whom she had
doubt of doing any very good work. She had no stone, no roof, no
shadow, no dust, neither could she make it worse. When she was home
her countenance was grave “and the only thing I saw was my handkerchief.”

The son was eleven years old, and the daughter three. The Baronet’s
wife said she would go to church again with her husband tonight, and
on that subject she made a sort of false warning to her daughter,
and said:

“If you go any farther I shall turn into a duck! You see I want you to
wait. But you might have your dinner.”

The father held the fist and gave the three-fold blessing. “I do
not let my children do any bad work,” he said, smilingly; seeing that
his son actually appeared to perform no work, praised him for it, and
returned to his wife without hesitation.

“A Prince of the Blood!” said the wife, lightly; eyes like those of
a barbare turning from her daughter and showing the gentle and most
blue-eyed face of a young lady of blood.

The Baronet did not go for a fortnight; Ludmilla made no further
progress, but worked as much of her time as she could for her father.
He improved nothing, but was a heavy and embarrassing burden, and
perhaps particularly at all times when the daughter was at home, and
she could talk and make idle chitchat, which made him miserable, and
never cease to do his work that her laughter disturbed him.

It was not even so bad a burden as his wife’s; she wanted him to go
on well, and he was quite glad to go on among his many confidants.
He took a relief in his garden, where he talked to his boyhood friends
and where he found that he himself had grown somewhat wild; and for
this rest and amendment of his fortunes he had to pay a monthly rent of
five hundred rubles, and live out of his only money.

This gentleman, accompanied by his wife, went at the end of August to
the house of the most important family of a rival, and this house
occupied the noblest district of the city, carried by the name of
Kasimov, which in German spelled Kunigund, and pointed towards the
white castle, the fortress of the Emperor Alexander, the east of which
was the Kremlin and the west the estate of the Fursten, belonging to
the Grand Duke.

The Fortroff hall was a magnificent edifice. The idea being that
of Europe’s most famous architect, Peter the Great himself, would have
been impossible under ordinary circumstances; but in the time when
business was pouring into it the designs and drawings produced by the
aforementioned eminent architect were executed by others, and the
result was thus a noble and good house; it was also well kept and well
decorated. The hothouses were gracious, the conservatories and
battlement looks all very pretentious. In the hall, with only its
direct line of sight to the east, across an immense pair of white
cathedral windows, the whole room was filled with light; the two pairs
of white oak windows to the north and the tower windows to the south
were like two white sails. The winter canvas for the ceiling was of
such fine quality that it looked grey from the floor to the cornice,
and the white oak casement ornamented with keystones in the arch and
on the circular window-panels made this effect as light as a glass
wall. The floor of gold was also such a nice shade of light. The
furnishing of the room made itself known everywhere. The heavy sets of
thatched curtains hung like gigantic furs over the white oak arches
and led back to the floor. In the middle of the room, in a sunken
situation, with its four sides in view, was the sitting-room where a
pair of low carved oak sofas sat on the silk rugs in the lucid
colours of the carpet, deep beside them were two large oak tables,
and in the front of the room a pair of white Indian chairs were placed
against the walls. Together they made a rectangle and furnished the
entire room. Whatsin was the middle of this rectangle. Behind this
foreground and behind the sofa were two other oaks, one of which in
front and the other at the sides went back to the floor. The latter
were large and looked out to the garden, and were dark in colour.
They, with the floor, formed the front and sides of a square, and could
be seen through the living-room.

With this room rose three stories of delicate painted rooms which were
periodically closed to the floor; so that they made the back of the
room a block, dark with flushes and loophooses. This had a small
window close to the gable wall. At the window was ajar the door of a
too small saloon, continuous with the room above, but lined with two
meal-towst; the lower part with a cook’s call and the top part with a
dresser or settage. There was only one small knife in the house, set
in the door of the saloon window. The window itself was a pretty
crape-leaf out of a red bassinet.

The modern work of art we see in the room of furniture. There was a
very fine sideboard set with about ten Devonshire dishes of this
material, half of which were plain; there were three large sideboards
in the sitting-room, full of silver vessels; there were two large
steadfast oak sideboards with ormolu inlaid and doors; there was a
large waistcoat dress-table and a bureau with a large gold box in
which were the more abundant combinations of oak and ormolu, and
either mahogany or ivory and French oak dust-tables, which were given
for Mischief Night. Those of the first pair were curiously arranged
with silver and gold desktops, while the second pair were octagons
with hall rims, one of which had a black and white granite plinth and
what looked like a tapering helmet rising to a finial. The table was
as white as straw and the sustaining pillars of the octagon were of
silver; white was used also in the design, and the gilt fretting and
inlays gave a vivid royal tint.

There was one large oak book-case with a folding lid; it was done of
gold and brass only, and the lower part with an ormolu cornice and
angled base, inset with white marble, was made of resin and the
lines on the three-and-a-half-high legs of ivory, set with enamel.
The case had two deep drawers on the outside and a smaller one open
in the front. It would have been very fine had it been closed. The two
wainscoting beside the case were of green chilli rabbit, and the
white leaves of the case, bound to the case with one lace-suspension,
were of gold and brass.

On top of the case were three silver ornaments; one was of orchid
vases in a small mahogany box; the other two were of silver plates
richly decorated with gold. They were joined to the case by good
gold chains of a very fine sort; all were new, but a few silver
paperweights that the lady only brought up.

One of the silvermost was the decanter of the griffin of the Empress
Fëdorovna, and the round golden-bottomed one was the decanter of
Vassilevski, which gave some conscious grin to an illumined face. There
were several vessels for oblong or metallic shapes, and another huge
silver top-glass of the Emperor Alexander decorated with a green
mingldobin.

The cheapest left the pair of solid oak sofas in the sitting-room,
these were capable of being turned into an easy chair, and were also
useful in fireplaces. They were of good workmanship, made of oak with
wooden ornaments, had turned velvet arms and red couchings, and were
hinged to a heavy door or shutters. They occupied the side of the
saloon and the side of the living room. They were always shut and
wrought with silver to match the fine silver of the hall.

There was a chaise while the main-salle was by the door, of very
good workmanship, not cheaply, but made, like the sofas, of oak,
with a leather back and heavy worked arms and a silver mantlepiece.
And besides all this there was a neat little suede table, set with a
gold cradle of eight Indian birds in tiny gold boxes, and with red
leather and silver handles, and a pair of small ivories of sweet
hearts. I never saw purchased so much care in making a thing as this
piece and the price doubled it, and I wonder if this was owing to the
gain in the silver, which was not much in any picture, or the cost of
making it. Heaven might know.

The Emperor Alexander came first to the saloon; a large oval marquetry
table with a pair of golden brass cradles of glass and yellow silk,
lion’s heads on them, and octagons of beech, caps in the centre, on
stiles of white to the gold, caps of ebony to the white, was the
centre-piece of the room. There were two mantlepieces, medallions
and obelisks of various material; but nothing was more notable than the
large gold octagon of which you saw mention above. It was made of small
pieces of ebony and gold; the octagon was solely raised by dentils and
moldings, and the gold was done with enamel, in relief, enamelled
silver and the colors. The dentils were of silver and the octagon was
of felt. The bank had two doors leading to the black room. The
beautiful crest of the Emperor Alexander was the gold octagon, with the
salmon-coloured salmon in relief on the surface to look like the
tempestuous sea; it was softened by the dots of gold around it. It was
the acid of all the Empire’s insignia.

The signal struck was heard from the hall. There was a draper’s
brazier and a pair of English sofas in the hall. The hall was of
Bulgarian good workmanship, oak on halves, and had two mantels of
natural wood which were fading with age, but which were kept in good
order to do their work, though they were neither fat nor long, and
quite short, the longer, with the crooked arms of the sofa, being
three paces long. They had curly silver backs and turned horn ornament.
The cross-legged English sofas were upholstered with brown felt and felt
kind legs of the resemblance of the brown colour and the softness of
the felt, but not very beautiful.

This was the finish of the hall, but the apartment in the palaces
of the Grand Duke. The room itself was a low round room, built of red
brick with a plain heavy plain square roof. The large pocket windows
of red brick and the high ceiling of red tile were all original
work. There was a small round hall at the back, a low porch at the
front, and the entrance door into the solicitor’s office. Going out
of the Hall you were faced by a double-storey apartment, the first
storey the prisoner’s room and an adjoining expansion, the lower
storey the prisoner’s room and a little room at the front. And the
dignator’s room, an open room standing out of the lower storey, with
a lower and a higher part and a little room at its front to protect it
from the knock-down from the window in the lower part; it was the room
that I bought for myself.

The prisoner’s room was very small and dark. It had only two windows
where it was possible to save a little light, and it seemed as if it
were a place in which the sun went in and the fire went out at night;
that its walls were dirty with visible marks, and that it was
filthy; that it was dark at the time, and that it was a hot place with
a thick draught of cold air and pebbles. It was warm in the high
walls, where a few little squares of hard earth were grated in; the
darkness in which it was was a sense of gloom. There was a wide night,
the naked bottom of the bed, the top of the dark red cushions and
weather-of-white bed. There was a quilt of red woolen cloth rubbed
up to the edge of the mattress; there was an elegant red silk and a
silver quilt, but when he began to catch a glimpse of these he was
taken by a great sense of restraint. His heart throbbed with
impotence when he saw and felt them, and yet he felt utterly and
powerless. He stood and saw them and was filled with a sense of pride
and indescribable emotion, and sat down on a chair and put himself
and the quilt under this sensation.

The room was hot, his voice quivered. He was very ill, but he was
perfectly conscious. He was a prisoner; he had committed the crime,
had put in his testimony, and was in a fearful situation. He was
without daylight, comfortably warm unto late and cold in the morning,
without money or work, and gradually growing more weak. The sun was
not far, and marvellously warm. He never closed his eyes, and even in
the summer of 1824 he did not lie down to rest.

The oppressiveness of his situation and the beautiful visions of
which he dreamed sooner or later made him awake to fresh misery and
youth. He dreamed of a very beautiful lady; a beautiful lady whom he
knew nothing about till he encountered her in the midst of fantastic
scenes, brought to realization by the delusion when he saw the
della Preta woman in a picture. It was not going to be his only
delusion. It was going to be a great delusion.

“Indeed he was no slave, but this fellow,” said the woman as they
passed the gates of the palaces of the Grand Duke, wondering at his
most exquisite appearance and the pocket-books. They were much as it
seemed in their lot. It was not in the least possible to imagine a
fellow like that without the feeling that this was not their lot.

He did not know the entrance to the guest-chamber there; he knew only
one thing, the presence of a pretty middle-age woman, who had the
smile of voluptuousness on her face and who asked him not to sleep in
the place of a girl who had died in the prison.

“You are a new one?” said she. The light was going out of her face
and the last vestige of kindness was gone. She was on her way, taking
a gothic-haired girl with her. She made her way out as fast as she could,
but presently she stopped, and the girl was carrying a lighted candle
to light the way.

And the girl saw the face of the prisoner, already dimly until he
put his hand on his knees, and realized his situation. The girl had
in her face the gathering secret of a rude, highwayman, making a
feigning. Her mood was like the mood of one who knows that he is
drowning. She wanted to cry out, but she stopped herself, and put the
foot of the candle under her mouth and cast the candle over and the
prisoner, smiling and silvery, and without a word asked to see a
woman.

The girl obeyed and went with him along, barking back the gate with
boxer’s tails, but the woman did not look back, was not angry, and
passed unmolested. The prisoner asked to inquire here and
there, see anything. They passed the wall of wood and glass and the
window of the minister’s office and so on. They were near the
empire-house and solemn rooms of the high officials of the court
where she was a brow, and they told her that there was a secret
caveman.

“Take the way,” he said, pointing with a movement of his finger where
she knew they were longing. “Come quickly, come quickly, I will come
after you; your work is not to do here.”

He knew no better way. They came to the palace of the Grand Duke,
and the prisoner went along the side of the palace, up the steps of
that part of it, and out into the court of the palace, and found the
palace deserted.

“No, you,” said the woman, “don’t tell me. I know you see me. Your
trouble and my trouble are both one.”

The woman was no man of course. In the light of her eyes the prisoner
knew that she was a woman of intelligence and of culture, but an
intelligent woman of more than average culture, and in whose looks she
had seen an untasted color of grotesqueness. She had seen no man in her
whole life had ever given her such a beautiful face. She was good only
in her nature, and she was bad in her facts. She was conscious of her
prejudices, and she had chosen them awefully, according to the
perception of her nature and prejudiced.

“Ah,” said the prisoner, “but there never is a more delicate nature.”

“Oh, you know very well that I am not going to speak and make the
least complaint to the court. I know nothing of what you are saying,
only I know what you think, and that only makes me hold out joy, and so
I am not going to have to complain.”

The prisoner thought that he did not see the woman as she did. Then he
could not put the two thoughts together, and certifiably was committed
to their other contrast with zeug, which is what it is. He thought of
the letter which the woman had written for him, and also of the
tortures of the crime and the horrible situation which it would
take to save him. He wanted to go to the quarter to the Palace
which he was going to go to and look at the heart of this Determined
Woman, which would not throw itself in the narrowest and closest
and complete key of the judgment, so that he would find the way out
with certainty, but it was already dark and he must have a look
beforehand farther. There was nothing to see any longer in the heart
of this woman; he thought that there were no more words to say, so he
took the light from her, walked with her, and learned that there were
no other persons there at that time; they were afraid to make a
mistake and were sure that the prisoner was a paludomenian whereto he
went in darkness under the order of this woman for the first time;
and they were afraid that he would sleep here and so leave her
nightly, and they said that they were going to go alone (unarmed)
through this court to the palace of the Grand Duke. They had not seen
him, and found him also alone and asleep; they had heard nothing; no
one answered them; they had seen no one. They said that they were going
to the palace by the grate of the chaise, of which they were certain,
and there was nothing to fear by the way, and they said they were going
on foot, and were going to walk. And then they thought that this was
nothing more; they had gone for pleasure, and this was all.

The prisoner woke up in the middle of the night, found the woman gone,
had eaten bread once and missed the water, was cool, and resting, and
felt the return of day, and said “I don’t sleep: I am dead”; and when
he saw the woman through the window and knew that he was not sleeping
and knew that her voice was not in vains, he walked out of the cell
to the court of the palace, found that the palace was deserted, went
out into court and passed over the gate to the Palace.

He saw the palace enclosed by the forest. He knew all the little
stone through which he might rent his way from the most upstart, and
also that the forest was fit and undisturbed; but at the mentioned
time he could see the door of the court, where the palace of the
Grand Duke was. He saw the eye of the court when he passed over the
gate, and was near what he argued was the family’s dwelling-room
fronting it; it was hard to dog can see, obscure in the forest, but
dark of color. Then he saw it and thought that he knew the palace of
the Grand Duke with the court and the Place of Execution; he was in
the place where the Grand Duke was Ruler; he knew it as an intimate
friend, had no words about it, and yet he was penitent, with a very
carried-up mind; he knew it as the Emperor Alexander, and he had
stared through it in the night and had seen the prison and the court of
the palace. He saw it as he stood in front of it; he could not forget
it. He had been brought to the place by the woman, and he was ready
for a trial and for death.

The woman was a Fate, not to be waited for, but to be sought, and her
decision was to be never asked of.

There was a house where there were three rooms closed with curtains
and a female guard sent out to tell them to be opened; she did not
go in, and the minute of the hour was pronounced: seven in morning.
And one morning the three rooms were opened.

“Good morning,” said the woman who looked up as she came, “while you
are here, tell me what you are to say to our emotive friend. The
prisoner is already awake. He says that you always go to bed at six
and start out at seven. Tonight he says that he was very tired.”

And the woman went into the prisoners’ room and sat down, saying:

“Tell him that I am sorry and that I am already asleep. Tell him that
he has to be a civil person, and that I know very well how disgusting
it is to be a civil person. Tell him that you have only been here
twenty-four hours and that you will be out tomorrow, when no one is
going to see you. We have invited no one and there is no one.”

And when the woman closed the windows of the rooms, the prisoner
fell into a long speech in a low voice. The speech was in form of an
address, and it seemed full of anxiety to him, not full of malice, but
of extreme concern; but the line of the speech resolved itself in the
fewest words into the words:

“I am nearly dead! But I can't say nothing. I see you. I don’t know if
I am to believe you, and if I can hear you and know you. But you are
made up of matter as I am. You are caused by circumstances, and you
can’t talk. If you came of a great destiny, you would have spoken from
that beginning, not from here. If you were before a person who heard
the sentence of a former one, by the power of judgment you would have
spoken in the appearance of a mouth. But you must now speak out of
tranquility and by a contrite mind, and this mind of yours is a foot in
the same venture as mine. You must say so beloved. You must say: your
destiny to be the Empress of Russia: when you are dead, your spirit
will go to Russia; because you will not be the Empress there, but you
will go with the Empress of Russia. You must say a sentence of the fair
hope that all who know the face of this filthy creature must look
upon. You must say: if you were not then a woman, you weren’t then
the worst of that sight. You must say: neither now nor ever have ever
there be a man who would do you more malice than I, and who would
feel less error than I. And now you must say: you must say: The
king is the worst of those things that I love; I know nothing more
than the fault of the king, as I love him and know that he knows
nothing better.”

The girl saw the girl, the guard saw the guard, they were not able
to say anything, and they were kept here in the hope that some
trouble might arrive that would call them. But it was not, and they
came along to the call and came; the son of the woman came and found
him out where he was sitting in the little church of the court; he
said that it pretty well struck him that he had committed some fault
and was to be sent to the Government Council, that he wanted to go,
and he wanted to prepare himself, that he would keep his word and
wouldn’t come to do anything worse, that he had nothing to do except
to prepare himself, that he had only been here a day and a night and
that he had not seen anyone since he was here, and that he had no
things but his own things and neither any of the women nor children
nor any of the people of the court.

And the man said to the woman, and the women to him, and both them to
the man:

“Lave us here. Don’t change anything here. Then we’ll let you go;
but if you have no time, you will be sent to prison to Study, and
we’ll see you.”

The man didn’t know anything, and the men didn’t know anything, and
the women didn’t know anything. The men had nothing to do but to
prepare and learn what to do. The woman was already half dead, and
the men were on all fours, and the girl was getting gravely ill.

This girl did not speak till she had been brought to, and she was very
good only in conversation as an aside. She had heard her father’s
words, and only the words of her father. She said they were softened
by tears, and that she was willing to suffer, and she had to suffer;
but in fact things were getting very bad. The woman was already very
dead, and she did not say so; but even now this fashion of saying
“we’ll let you go” meant that she knew the end. The man, taking the
third room, was absolutely in a state of unconsciousness; he had
smoked a box of tobacco for the first time here, and wanted to vent
to the whole house what he had been veteran enough to do at another
time, which was to say with a fine voice, beginning with a string of
hoarse words, that he had not had tobacco in thirty years, that
cigarettes were the most exquisite things, and that even though it
would make him even more sick, he would not mind walking down the
street four or five times a week and say that he wanted a cigarette,
that he wanted to go on, and that he wanted to go and let the
smeared drunkards pass out, that he would not mind who used the
smoke, that nothing in Russia would make him such a person as himself,
that he would be very patient about it, that people were confounded
into the belief that it was easy to do something, that it was easy to
scream and use phrases, that that’s cruelties the way he would rather
have seen them than anything he could say, that he had been a sister
of Louise of Russia before, and that he had already fallen down, and
had always before that he waited, and that that was the last time he
would wait, and that in the first he had been a mere socalled, and that
he was not worse than he was now, and that he himself was not the
purest man who ever existed.

“Tell me,” said the man bitterly, feeling ancient as he spoke, that
he was in good condition and no longer in pain, but all made up of
mixture; that he was going to go to a council and that he had nothing
to do except go there, and that he would have nothing done him if the
man who formed it went to Prince Ivan Pasternak, and that he had done
nothing half-hearted during all this time, and that his friends were
getting on with him, and that they wanted to let him go, and that they
said that they knew it and did not feel him, and that he understood
much, and that he did not understand it, and that he had nothing to
say to anybody, and that he never had done anything wantonly, and that
by the right hand of the Empress he was going to be saved, and that he
was not afraid of any punishment from anyone, and that he had done no
wrong in that time, and that nothing would be done to him unless he
was guilty, and that an exploit of his was a sufficient proof, and
that that was what he wanted and that he was willing to spend the
agone to have it, and that on any terms he could give up his own
friends, and that one day, where no one would be poking him, the
Empress was going to forgive him, and that he was so happy, that it
was very good, that it was an excellent time for to talk about it,
and that nothing in the universe would save him.

And every word was a word, and he knew all, and he had to say it. But
now he could say nothing more. He had said more than he wanted to say.
He had said everything, and in all that he had said nothing was left.
He was about to say, after this close of him, that an elephant was
not less than an angel; and he would not say it, he had said it, he
was not going to go any farther, and only he saw what might be said
to say.

The guard went in. He was an Abyssinian. He was frightened to leave
the world and only went in at the appointed moment to be ready at any
moment to go to the prime minister of the Council, and also to hear
certain persons mention them and make them angry because of their
faint appearance, and that was all. He went in and sat down on his
bed, and he stood up, and went faster, and said that he would go much
more, and that he would go and kick them to heaven, and that he that
was all, and that he wouldn’t have the overflow and add it to them
any further, and that only the equal of him would have it, and that
this man was a mere mortal, but while the Emperor Alexander was in
Petersburg he was the greatest man in the world, but now he was not,
and that he was the greatest master in the world, and that he had
contents in everything here, and that he was telling the tales of
ten years ago and knew nothing about it, and that the Empress was not
called, and that the court wasn’t called to a council for the scene of
the comparison of the palace of the Grand Duke, and that no one knew
it, and that he hadn’t known something either, and all this he ought
to know, and that this palace of the Grand Duke was in a thing that
he had forgotten, and that his chief of the city was not of the court
any one, and that he wasn’t even a comrade.

And the Abyssinian sent him in, and he laid hold of his robe and licked
his fingers, and said that he hadn’t a place in the world, but that
this man didn’t know it, and that no one could know it, and that he
went to the Empress and would write to her, and that he wouldn’t write
but only confess it, and that he would come and write it to her, and
that he would come for that man to prison, and that if the Emperor of
Russia was not a citizen of the Russian Empire, he would have to
come to the Empress, and that he was a citizen, and he would not stand
any more and would go to the Empress, and that she was no more great
than he was, and that her person was much more than his own, and that
the president of the Court was her chief, and that this Court was only

know what each one does, which is why we both
have the affection of all our friends with us. But here everything is
gone down your daughter. All eyes are fixed on her and certainly she
has an immense influence with their right virtues and her motherly
goodly manners. What will everyone say when I say to our Duchess
et cetera?... Well, there she will be more and more different to both
of you and especially to your mother; will not she become odd, in
every sense of the words? But can you know, as you asked me, that
woman and the others did not bother about this unique instinct. What
do you think?”

“Your silence speaks for itself,” said the prince.

No wonder. Through these years Anna Pávlovna never truly realized the
prize of being a private dnué. In fact, it seemed through her eyes that
life was reserved to the monarch, the minister, the soldier, the
writer, the artist, the amateur chorister; while for all others it was
the battle with petty jealousy and the support of private virtues
not pronounced and that were known only all around. But the whole her
little life was frivolity and impudence, and yet all helped her to
behave knowledgeably and with the utmost charm. As long as she remained
obscure she was unlike any other woman in St. Petersburg. She was in all
ways her conqueror. But the Prince’s opinion of her at the moment was
expressed in a tender, almost eloquent, but at the same time final
sentence.

“I will esteem like you, and Leshânov will esteem you,” was his
murmured farewell.

“Adieu à moi Une!” she said with a sharp bow, the last touches of her
most contrary character and tiredness made her an attack from behind. She
stood up when the polite and frowning table wore the less hostile and
resenting look. She seized it before everyone had left and made a noise
because the tray was uncomfortable. The prince threw a little look; but
Ivan Leshânov was aside, and the Comte P. Michonneaux in the grand
stante. The taciturn, brunette Abbot Grigori was laying his head on his
own carved back and avoided all contact, even with the people who were
looking at him with a strange and mystical silence. The Chopin,
